div.head: LADIES' LE'TTEII.
div.p: LADIES' LE'TTEII.

1- 7 DEAR NaLLIE, Hats and toques are of the most airy descrip• tion, many of them merely wire mounts swathed In tulle and areophane ; others are of crin, a thin yet wiry substance which is capable of being bent and cajoled into any form desired, and is sufficiently dressy looking to need little further adornment. It is more durable for the larger hats if the crin is stitched in rows upon a straw founda- tion; this is quite hidden, the surface showing nothing but the crin, but the wearing results are infinitely better. Another new make of straw is very closely plaited with a dull surface fike rice- straw, and promises to be a good deal more used for the large picture and bebe hats; the more floppy the straw the better it seems adapted to the requirements of fashion. The danger in these large careless sort of hats is the risk of their givmg an untidy look to the wearer. They need the utmost dressing up to, and a suitable time and ace for the wearing of them, otherwise tliq result 14 Hit reverse of smart.

Chiffon continues to be the staple material of the evening blouse. A good way to adapt the jetted y0kt...3 and sleeves bought at the winter sales is to have a half-high chiffon blouse made, the yoke and elbow sleeves to be added on, the latter supple- mented by frills of the chiffon. The elbow sleeve has entirely ousted the long variety, and well- shaped arms have again a chance of being seen. When dances begin again, short sleeves will come in. They are now divided into two portions, one crossing the shoulder like a brace, the other droop- ing upon the arm almost in a line with the top of the bodice. For use during the present month a number of beautiful black embroideries have been produced. Many of them have all the effect of fine lace, and these are used to trim evening bodices, and to edge the little boleros that so often form part of them. These very becoming little addenda will not soon be allowed to drop out of fashion. They are sometimes bordered with fringes, either jet or silk. The beaded fringes are all coming in again.

Revers on coats and jackets seem to have merged thernsels into the collar, and ceased to have a separate existence; the collar is deep and ronnd, and invariably turned down; with boleros it is usually tied in the centre with large important bows of tulle or ribbon. The bolero bide fair to be übiquitous this spring, in cloth, in corded silk or satin, and in panne it assumes many guises, of which the most pleasing is the banded, pouched Russian Mouse kind, but the newest that milli coat taste behind. Very decorative belts are nossusede with a gdd ioution embroidered in turquoise idne and coral pink, with a little pale oliveand russet brown for subduing the brightness-4 colours. Some of the prettiest belts are in Mask boa lined with a fold of white chiffon again with a firm band of black silk. The mob are wired in loops at the back, and then fall-over the dress.

The raison d'iltre of a turned back cuff, which I saw on one dress, is to free the hand. G.vnike- quently the turn of the elbow is the v.Tong place for it. The undersleeve in this case is puffed lace. The sleeves in one lady's for day dresses had the undersleeve carried up well to the elbow, the other portion just turning it. The evening dresses had all very short sleeves, a fact that may interest those who are doubtful if short sleeves have not been entircly displaced by long, transparent ones. Ribbons are to play a very important part in dress as sashes, Watteau bows, Empire scarves, ends to ruffles, and loops to boleros and in the soft gauze makes form the sole trimming to mourning hats in the shape of large, seemingly careless bows. The patterns and colourings of the newest ribbons forms an endless variety; but, perhaps, the prettiest are those with a sort of lace background, patterned with silk woven roses and other flowers, and those with a rich satin graund inlet with ap- pliques of lace. Many have a gold or silver thread running through the whole of the weaving, and some are of gauze, puckered up by lines of the gold thread at half-inch intervals. Broad sashes of lace, with wide rounded ends, springing from nothing seems to accord better with the tender green and fleecy clouds which suceeed the darkness and dreariness of winter, but mauve promises to be the more fashionable. The combination of grey and mauve is a pretty one, and sufficiently un- common to be attractive. Mauve has hitherto been the colour of the few, for it is not universally becoming, and there is an old prejudice against it on acconnt of the saying that the woman who wears mauve is not to be trusted. Fashion will probably prove stronger than fancy. The en- deavour to include red as a half-mourning tint is not likely to obtain a following; it is an old id- but a more or less incorrect oue, and the mere that the combination of a bright red and black is not a pleasing one, too voyante a contrast, is against it. The plain skirt wins all round as yet, closely fitting at the top, very full at the feet, this fulness being likely to increase as time goes on. Your loving JENNIE.

The full accounts from Gibraltar report that the Ophir bad a very rough passage, as far as the Mediter- racean, and, unfortunately, the Duchess of Cornwall and York is one of the poorest sailors of the, Royal Family. The Queen is also anything but a good sailer, and Her Majesty had to postpone her departure for Denmark, on account of the rough weather. That distressing inflic- tion mat-de met, is no respecter of r e rsons, and though all kinds of remedies, or supposed remedies, were not . wanting, it is quite clear that norm are reliable, or else • we may be very sure they would be found for such dis- tinguished sufferers as the Queen, and the Duchess of Cornwall and York. Dr. Manby who has long acted as surgeon apoi.beeary at Sendringhain,and who is on board the Ophir, took every conceivable remedy for sea sick- ness with him, but apparently, with no better results than usually attend these efforts to relieve those who are unaccustomed to the sea. The Queen and her sister the Doseager Empre, a of Russia, will be the guests of the King of Denmark for about a month, and the King is also expected at Copen- hagen for the celebration of King Christian's eighty third birthday ore April 8. Afterwards the King will go to Homburg for two or three weeleowhile Queen Alexandra will pay some family visits in Germany, includeig ore to the Empress Frederick at Briedrichstiof. Th. King of Denmark is now the only octogeoarian among the principal Sovereigns of Europe. The oldest representa- tive of our own Royal Family, is, of course, the Duke of Cambridge, who has just entered upon his eighty-third year. It is exactly 100 years since the Dulecdom of Cambridge was conferred upon his father in 1801, and though several members of our Royal Family have lived to be octogenarians, none have lived to so great an age as the present Duke of Cambridge. The Dowager Duchess of Argyll is busily engaged upon the life of leer late husband, and the Argyll memoirs should Contain many interestirg chapters on the Duke's relaticnships with Queen Victoria, and with most of the distinguished men of his time in the religious. scientific, and political walks of life. Family differencps account for the fact that the present Duke is not his fathee's literary heir, but, though disappointed in this respect, , he will be able to give more time to his present work on the life of Queen Victoria. Last week the Duke dele I brated the thirtieth anniversary of his marrage with Princess Louise, who, though ber talents lie more in drawing and eculptureeis a great help to her besband in his present work on the life of her late Majesty. The Duke and Ductiess of File will open the Glasgow International Exhibition on the 2nd ofeiday, a few days earlier than was arranged. For three years Glasgow has been organising and preparing for the first gee, t Ex- I hibition of the new Century, and though it is not upon the same gigantic scale as that of Paris last year, it has I aroused scarcely less interest among foreign nations, and it will be sure to attract many visitors to the North In London we are to have a great Military Exhitition at Earl's Court which is to be opened early in May. under the patronage Of the Duke of Cambridge, and Earl Roberts. There will be many illustrations of the manufactur- ing of war material, and its uses. Also an interesting exhibition of war relics,including mementos of Napoleon I. down to General Baden Powell's collection of trophies from Senth Africa, which has not yet been exhibited to the public. Many exhibits have also been lent by the French Government, illustrating the military service in France. In the Empress Theatre, which holds 5,000 persons, there will be a grand military spectacle, en- titled "China or the Relief of the Legations." Alto- eether the Earl's Court season promises to be a great Success and a new scheme has been devised under which part ot the proceeds will be devoted to the Soldiers and Sailors Help Society, This year we seem to leave had an unusually long spell of cold winds and bleak skies, which are se trying to one's complexion. Everyone will welcerne a change to more genial conditions, for which the shopkeepers appear to be waiting before malting any great display of new spring fashions. So far, though the period of public mourning is almost over, there appears to be a general disinclination to drop the more sombre attire which has been universal since January. The weather toss been all against early changes, for it is seldom that wee arrive at April with so few signs of spring about,and people having laid in a stock of black seem disposed to make the most of the opportunity to wear out their mourning garments. Some even suggest that women , having discovered bow much easier it is to dress in black, will net go back to all tbe varying changes in colours and styles which Dame Fashion demands - Men, they say, seldom bother themselves about more than a simple contrast in white and black, but only the most sanguine among us would expect to live to see such simple and stereotyped ideas adopted by our sex. Not long since, a black tea gown was deemed an im- possibility, from an artistic point of view. But we have changed our views upon the subject, and the black tea gown is now the smartest of smart wear. Chiffon enters largely into the composition of the best "creations," but this is costly wear, stud only a possibility to these whose pnne strings are elastic. For the less well-Jowered how- ever' there remains tbe soft inexpen.ive type of satin, with which we are all now familiar. This needs to be mounted on firm but stiff sateen, which does not crease and wears excellently. The Princess shape is the favorite of the moment, and, from beneath the slightly open Coat, a front of black net, embroidered with black sequins, and mounted on the plain satin looks particu- larly well, The addition of some black laae is all that Is necessary to complete this fascinating garment. Tucked chiffon is giving place to tucked tulle, and many of tbe best teques and big picture hats, are entirely of the latter, two or three sweeping ostrich plumes, and a jet or steel buckle, being the most ap- proved form of trimming for such headgear: With regard to flowers, the newest have each petal veiled in chiffon, the effect beitig exquisitely soft. Wbite flowers veiled in black, and black floaters veiled in white, are being much used by leading milliners, at the moment, and such blooms go far towards rendering the electiou a SUCCESS. Quite narrow collar bands have appeared in some of the latest " corsages," by which title our old familiar friend the blouse is now known. These narrow bands are doubtless infinitely better for our health, and the beauty of our neck, but they are not styleful, and those women who have adopted the idea may generally be seen wearing a high velvet bend abeve—more or less adorned with jewelled slides—which are very few de- grees less harmful from the beauty doctor's point o view, than the I igh stiff collar of olden times. Still take us altogether we are much more .hygenic, as regards muffling up our throats than we used to be,and the more sensible among us will, in this particular instance avoid extremes, and patronise the collar band of medium width, that requires no band above it. Core corners are out of date. In their place now appear wide, low seats, tightly covered with material, the curved legs being well in evidence, no valance of Any kind being permissible. And all monster Cushions have been banished from the drawing-room. As usual we have rushed off to the opposite extreme, coma of the s'-called cushions, appearing in fashionable apartments, having almost reached vanishing point. There are how- ever less dust traps about drawing-rooms than formerly, sn item whereat to rejoice. Draperies over fire-places and doors, round pots, and photograph frames, etc., have Vanished, let Us trust to be no more seen. "MADGE." ; DR. ADAMS AND A DECREASFD -BIRTH RATE. The annual repert orDr Adams, medical officer to tile Runcorn Rural District Ceuncil, has just been issued. The number of deaths registered during the past year was 390. but 21 of these were of persons belonging to the Runcorn Urban District who died in Dutton Work. house. The births uumbered 629, of which 314 were males and and 315 females. The rate per thousand was equal to 27 6. This says Dr Adams, is a distinct decrease on the average birth-rate of the last ten years, viz.. • 271 per thousand of the estimated population. In 1891, for instance, the birth-rate was 311, "This decennial lowering of the birth-rate" he says, "is a serious matter, alike for the limited area of the Council and for the whole country. Its final tendency in towards a stagnant population, as exhibited by a neighbouring • country where births and deaths may almost challenge each other in the scales of the statistician.. The causes of this are difficuit to ascertain. There is increasing gravitation towards towne I and cities by the youths in agricultural areas, reflecting only the decreasing buying power or their wages by such indirect incidence of taxation as press most heavily upon them in proportion to a probab - ircrease of wage earning power, such as taxed comm 0 I elides like tea, sugar, tobacco, &e. But of this I know nothing, and Em at present only disposed to think that the tendency towsrda a decreasing birth-rate in rural districts is net a temporary incident but a more or less permanent factor in our social life, to be studied with care allke by District Councils and the Government to whom they are responsible." Referring to the need of an isolation hospital, Dr Adams says the question has been in abeyance during I the last year. It necessity, however, is as great as ever, especially in view of the fact that the adjoining districts of Chester and Warringiain are no longer able or willing to afford accommodation for even your worst and most pressing cases. Applications are occasionally made to me, of an urgent character, to negotiate for the removal of such cases, but the nego- tiations have always latterly resulted in disappointment. Seventeen cases of diphtheria were notified and six deaths occurred as compered-with 37 cases and only 2 deaths in the previous year: The most serious outbreak was in Tbelwall. This will probably form the sutject of a Local Goveonment Board incyriry at an early date. During the year, the Warrington Corporation obtained the necessary powers to extend the waterworks system further into your district, and your Council acquiesced in the arrangement: This extension, when carried out, will prove a great benefit 'to Batton, Stretton, and such contiguous areas as will be traversed by the extended water mains. In last year's report I spoke of defective arrangemsuts for rem sal of night Soil. In Stocktan H .ath these defects have been remedisd to some extent by employment of another contractor; but other areas in your district are in muah need of improvement in this respect.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDILY
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDILY
(Copyright.) -RUBY LOVEDAY 4/c.'
By siaß K: ilooKlgG, Author of "The Strange Adventures of Israel Pendray," "The Day of Recompense," "God's Outcast,!' '!ln Spite of Fate," Her Benny," &a "'CHAPTER XXlr:
TIIE COURSE OF LAW. "Law and equity are two things which God hath joined,: But which man hath put asunder." 4 - -

In theory, as everyone knows, the law is a beautiful thing. In practice an adjective of a very different kind is needed to Ocribe it. Ostensibly laws are made in the interests-of truth and justice; in reality they are made in the interests of the lawyer and the man with a long Final' _There is a fable that has been long current, amongst us that every man can have justice in this highly favoured landrind so he can if he is able to -pay for but as comparatively few people are able to do that tit followslhat justice ist a very unfamiliar presence in many quarters, whilst the Law Courts are as much dreaded as a highway robber. -Mr. Jacob - Bice knew a good deal about lair. He had been trained.imit from his youth. He had a certain admiration for it as a stable-boy has for a skittish horse; its unexpected'pranks and caper- ing,s. were interesting. What it. required was management. There was nothing...fixed or rigid about it Many people fancied so, Init.thatras a mistake; it was as pliant and elastic as e-piece pf india-rubber,_but,,of_sourse,.it required a shrewd man to turn it the right way. In Mr. Rice's mind justice and law,had little Or no connection. They were entirely separate and distinct. -Justice was a matter that he had no concern for and took no interest in. The beauty of taw was that it enabled you to evade justice and give it the go by. As a lawyer he cared nothing for mere abstract questions of truth, and right, and equity. Bare, obvious facts that could not be twisted or distorted were a nuisance from his point of view. He liked to be able to write a query opposite every statement, then he could get his wits to work, and perhaps set the machinery of the law in operation. He always rejoiced when he saw the slow movements of its wheels. His chance came then. The lawyer was always safe to win whatever happened. It might be grinding widows and orphans to. death and branding honest men as felons, and‘lifting, rogues and rascals into high places. That was no concern of his. The business of the clever inner was to prove—by the aid of this wonderrul machine —that wrong was right, that truth was falsehood, and that justice was a public scandal. In the past he had rarely any cause to complain of his good fortune. Ostensibly he had worked in the interest of Lord Tregeegle, but while he had increased his employer's rent-roll, he in added very considerably to his own professional 'lncome. He had enclosed hundreds of acres of common land in the parish, and in the few cases where Lord Tregeagle's right had been disputed he had come off victor. He had evicted More than one would- be freeholder from his small estate, and had made the law such a terror to poor people generally that , when he threatened them with its consequences they usually yielded up their- rights without another word. , The outcome of his encounter with John'Pentyre was, in his own mind, a foregone conclusion. In a few days at most he would see the farmer igo• under the wheels, then he would have his revenge. His surprise, therefore, was all the greater, and his indignation' beyond expression when, on the second morning after his • abortive attempt at eviction, he was served with a summons for trespass and with unlawfully attempting to, break into John Pentyre's'housi. I At first he Could hardly credit his own senses. Then he raved and swore tilt he wail =nearly bliick in the face. Finally he condescended to make inquiries. • • ' 7 1 There was no illegality about the sum. 'us, and, rave as he might, he would have to a.. -• before the magistrates and answer to the ge. Of course, he would be able to prove his right in five minutes; but it was terribly annoying nevertheless. It stayed the process of eviction,' it made it appear to the parish as though John Pentyre had check- mated him. For the moment he would be the laughing-stock of every man and boy in the district. He wondered what Nankivel could mean by taking service for John Pentyre against him. And he rushed off to Trelford to consult hie fellow-lawyer. Nankivel was as surprised as he. "I assure you," he said, "I have heard nothing about the matter till this moment." • "Then Pentyre has employed a fresh lawyer?" "It seems so," he said. "Between ourselves I don't wonder," was the cynical reply, "but I wonder what's at the bottom of it." I "Perhaps Symons knows," said Nankivel, ' lugubriously ; and he touched a ben for his head' • clerk. Symons came at once. "Have you heard anything about the Pentyres, of Endilloe, since yesterday ? " Nankivel questioned. "Well, yes, sir. I hoard something as I came along this morning, but I don't know if there is any truth in it. "What did you hear ?" "Well, it is reported that young Pentyre drove over to Truro yesterday afternoon and brought back Lawyer Hendy with him. It is also said that they have found the deeds which were missing." "Great Heavens, no!" Bice ejaculated. "I'm only repeating what I heard as I came along, sir." Mr. Bice did not wait to hear any more but hurried away at once to his own office, and within half an hour he was in possession of all the facts of the case. Later in the day he consulted his chief. Lord Tregeagle rubbed his chin for a moment, then smiled. "in law, I think I have heard you say, Bice, it is the longest purse that wins ?" "That is so, my lord." "Then in this matter I think we need not trouble ourselves." "Not in the least, though, of course, as you know, law charges are always heavy." "Yes, I am aware of that. You lawyers know how to bleed people. Still, we cannot afford to allow ourselves to be defied by a farmer; the thing I is intolerable." "We'll soon get to the ,aid of his tether, my lord, and then his little game will be up." "But do you think his title is of any value?" "It may be all right in equity, Sir, but what we have to do is to shew that it is no good in law. That need not be difficult. You can command the best talent, and if the worst comes to the worst you can starve him out. When his lawyer finds that he has no more money he will throw up the case." “Well, Bice, we have gene so far in this matter now that we are bound to carry it through to the end." So the enterprise was sanctioned, the sole end and object of which was to rob an honest man of his rights and to reduce him to a position of abso- lute subjection. In the innocence of his heart John Pentyre imagined that the matter would be settled in a week or two at the outside, and settled to his entire satisfaction. So once more he was supremely happy, and went singing to his work as though all life's troubles had come to an end. Tom Pendarvis established himself at St. lago, Churchtown as consulting engineer and calmly waited for Clients. He was not eager for work to come to him with a rush, for he had brought more money with him from Airica than he would be able to spend for many a year, and, besides that, he was by no means anxious that the time he spent with Dorothy should be needlessly curtailed. bevertheless, as some of his inventions became ,known, work crowded in upon him, and without effort on his part he soon 'beeama a person of con- siderable influence in the neighbourhcod. Justin felt almost resentful sohietimes when he saw Tom and Dorothy walking away together across the fields in the quiet of the summer evenings, or panic upon them sitting on the cliffs watching the sun go down. He felt like a bird that had lost its mate, and time, instead of lessening the sense of his loss, seemed to increase it. I. Now that Endilloe had settled- down to its normal state Of 'calm and the long tension had come to an :end, he had time to brood again over the hope that had gone out of his life. So month by month passed away. Little by little plant was laid down. Day by day order steadily grew out of confusion. First this machine was got to work, then that, till at length the first batch of ore was "stamped," "dressed," and sold, and then the whole district knew that Wheal Patience was a huge success. The directors met and recommended the first dividend, and a general meeting of the shareholders was called for the following week. Justin worked early and late in preparing his report' and his mother saw, with no little anxiety, that he was exhausting his strength all too rapidly. "What is the use, Justin," she said, "of gaining the world, and losing your life over it? "No use at all, mother," he answered, pathetic. ally. "But why do you do it?" "I hope I am not doing it; besides, I am going in for a long rest when the general meeting is over." He did not know how pathetic his words were. We often speak as seers without knowing it. The general meeting was called for two o'clock. It seemed to many a red-letter day for the whole neighbourhood. Everyone was in the best of spirits, and eager to hear the manager's report. Also a little proposal was on foot to present Justin with a handsome honorarium in consideration of the amount of work that he had done during the past twelve months. While waiting for the clock to strike, the share- holders broke up into little knots and discussed Wheal Patience ; discussed the price of tin, dis- cussed Justin, discussed everything, in fact, that bore in any way upon the object of their meeting. On the whole, Justin came in for the larger share of attention. In the eyes of many he was regarded as something of a phenomenon. By his persistence and energy it was believed he had wrested Endilloe from the grasp of Tregeagle, and certainly by the same qualities he had discovered and developed Wheal Patience. great future, and wondered Several of the older mend where eicted he fwoorulhdimlivae and whom he would marry, and how he would spend his money. From a matrimonial point of view, he was regarded as the best catch in the neigh- bourhood; and the wonder grew daily that, with all his opportunities, he elected to remain a bachelor. Had they known the sweet and tender romance that he kept locked up in his heart, they would But they did not know. have remained silent. Justin was true to his ideal. He had loved once, he could not love again. The clock struck at length, and Justin had not arrived. This was most unusual, for he was one of the most prompt and punctual of men. In an ante-room the directors looked at their watches, and wondered what the manager had done with himself. A quarter of an hour passed away, and still Justin had not put in an appearance. Then one of the directors started out to make inquiries. He had gone underground about ten in the morn- ing, but no one had seen him return. Then sarch was made in his private changing- room, which left no doubt that he was still under- ground. By this time the anxiety had become general, and a dozen men had quickly volunteered to go under- ground in search of him. The meeting of the shareholders broke up in confusion; and in half- an-hour all St. lago knew that Justin Pentyre was missing, and that it was feared some accident had befallen him.

div.p: CHAPTER XXVI.
GAIN AND LOSS. r 11' Work is not man's punishment. It is his reward."

justin had awaited the conclusion of the trial with intense eagerness. During the time he had been business manager for the Bassett brothers, he had made one or two discoveries, ' the most im- portant being that the main east and west tin lode, which had proved such a treasure-trove to the Bassetts, would, in the ordinary course of thing, run under a considerable portion of the Endilloe estate; and if it was so rich in tin on the Tres- kiddy side of the valley, there seemed no reason why it should not be equally rich on the other side. Of course, this did not always follow. A lode that was a perfect gold mine in one field might, when it passed into the adjoining field, be absolutely worthless. Moreover, though lodes usiially ran a pretty direct course, there were many puzzling and unfortunate exceptions. From the fact that there were shafts in a corner of the Endilloe estate, it seemed clear that very many years before somebody had made a search for the lode on that side of the

valley and had failed to find it. That did not prove, however, that it did not exist. A " fault " might have lifted it out of its proper course; but "faults" did not usually destroy lodes altogether. The more Justin thought about the matter, the more he felt convinced that the Treskiddy "East and West," as it was termed, ran under the Endilloo estate, and that the man who was fortunate enough to discover it would make a fortune. Hence Justin's anxiety for the trial to end was far keener than he let anyone know, and when at length his father's title was established beyond all dispute, he set to work at once to find the hidden
_ treasure. He made the old shaft—which he had descended
years before in search of treasure of a different kind—the basis of operation. "Driving" in opposite directions, he concluded that the lode was certain to be struck sooner or later.

So the anxious days passed away, and grew into weeks, and the weeks into months, and the report from underground was always the same. No sign of the lode was visible in either direction. Justin's father adviml him to abandon the project; and more than once he was on the point of taking his father's advice, but his native tenacity of purpose came to his assistance. Having carried the search so far, it would be humiliating to give up now. It was true he had exhausted all his savings, and was borrowing from Tom Pendarvis, who was banker for the family. True also that at time hope almost failed him. And yet—and yet, for all he knew, he might be within a few inches of the coveted treasure.

"I'll try one week mor'e," he said one day to his father, "and if that fails, then I think I'll give up. and own myself defeated." The neat day, while they were at dinner, two miners in their working ,attire Came into the room unannounced. "We've foun' un, maaster," they said, and they dived their hands into their pockets and brought out some splinters of rock. Justin sprang to his feet in a moment, his whole frame quivering. "Have, you struck the lok ?" he cried. "lee, maaster, we've cut 'n sure 'nough; an' a beauty tee to." "Is this some of the ore?" he asked. "Aye, ruaaster. Jest hould it up to the light an' look at it. Ain't it lovely ?" "But these are picked samples surely ? " ; "No, master. There's tons and tons of the I .ante kind. Why. bless 'ee. maaster. the ' end' is

Stockton. Heath Representation on the ~Distri Council. Sir,—l read in your contemporary of last Saturday an account of the . attendances of our District Councillor (Mr C W DatrenportOortho last- three years of office just expiring. le at electors in this *Octant and fast growing parish Of Stockton Heath are called upon to elect by ballot on Monday next a representative for another three years' upon the Runcorn Rural District Council. Now Mr Editor and fellow ratepayers I do protest as a ratepayer and prrperty owner against giving the honour of representation to any man whoever be be who will not'attend to the duties thereof. We see by t figures given. last Saturday that our representative 18C8 cirt eta possible 26 meetings only attended 8 1E99 „ „ 26 / • 29 6 1900 . .. 26 1 1931 hp to Feb. 26 „ 5 „ „ „ 0 83 15 I consider this an injustice to the electors in the pat, and moreover the same gentleman is again coming for ward and soliciting the votes and support of intelligent electors for another three years to represent (?) es upon that important Council. I ask Mr Davenport in all fairness if he conifers this a fair representation as I for one fail to see what claim he hil upon the further support and confidence of the ratepayers. The attendances are wow the nearer the time comes for offering himself for re-election. I appeal to the electors to give their support to Mr Pemberton who will give the time, and has the ability, energy and inclination to serve the true interests of the rate- payers and not neglect them. Remember the rates are steadily advancing and not reducing as they ought. Let him take the honour of representation who is pre- pared to do the work and not shirk it. Yours truly, FAIR PLAY.
THE FREE cimibri GIRLS' GUILD.
The main work of the National Council -,

during the coming year will be the organisa:, tion of Girls' Guilds el over ,the county. The constitution of the Guild vas 'adopted hist year at Sheffield, but it soon became apparent that the Councils could not simultaneously carry out two such great schemes as the Mission and the Guild, and it was resolved to hold over ,the Guild work until the Mission was ended. The Free Church Girls' Guild will simply' be aGirls, Friendly Society, permeated with Free Church principles, but not used or proselytising pur- poses. Miss Hearn (" Marianne Farningham of the Christian World) made a delightful tipeech at Cardiff in advocacy of the Guild.

" Mercury " and the Board of Guardians Election. Sir,—l cannot compliment your correspondent " Mercury," on his letter in your last issue, nor on his non de plume. Be should at least be " q 3icker " to ,ascertam facts before rushing into print. He speaks of I die "alleged" compact between the two political parties. It seems as if " Mercury "had been emulating Rip Van Winkle, not to know this fact• He says the Trades and Labour Council is largely composed of insurance agents. Had he applied for in- formation at the right source he would have learned there is only one insurance agent delegated to that Council by his society. And oh, the crowning state- ment which stamps" Mercury's" letfer as ignorant, if not amuSing is the temark that "Warrington has nine guardians to elect." I think every novice in local politics could tell him Warrington elects ten represents- rivf son that Board. From the foregoing, your readers will not, I think decide that " Mercury" is a qualified judge of what constitutes " the solid grounds of per- sonal fitness and ability" about which be talks so much in his letter.—Yours, Zee., P. J.

Sir' —I desire to reply to some of the statements made by "Mercury "in the " Examiner " of last Saturday. To deal with all the questions to which be refers would take morn space than I data ask for. In regard to the • alleged ' compact, let me say that it was not an alleged " compact, but an actual agreement between a few officials of each political party " that for two years neither party should oppose the other when a vacancy occurred on the Town Council. " Circulars I were sent out by both parties, informing the electors of that decision. If further proof is needed, let me ask 1" Mercury" if it is not a fact that prominent members of both parties worked in support of Mr & Jolley in Latchford Ward when he was returned to the Council. The same thing happened in Orford Ward last year. The reason given for this procedure was" that both parties oad agrefd to oppose any candidate who should be nominated for the 7 own Council." Your correspondent tells us that " he does not think governaoent by party is the best form of administra- tion," but in his ineousistency he says "He sincerely hopes that the two political parties will see to it, tha& on every OeCkSibe they will bring out the best men thel have,and don't let eitherparty oppose the nominee of the otlier for political reasons.' Candidates selected by political parties are very often selected snore for expediency than for fitness. It is thereforr questionable whether the interests of the town will be best served by rho political parties acting on the not very intellig.-nt suggestions of your correspondent " Mercury." The methods of the two parties have been largely responsible fur the lack of interest shown in local elections by the working men of Warrington. In his letter " Mercury" also complains of the action ,f the Trades and Labour Council and of its constitution. He states that "it would be interesting to know how many insurance agents, there are on that body, for from the reports of the Council's meeting.s. lam of an opinion that it is largely composed of that class of men." It is doubtful whether he has ever read a report of the Trades Council meetings. If he had he would not make such an absurd statement. If it would be "interesting to know these things.ard I am sure it would be"interest ing "to know who this genius "Mercury " is. and if he will allow his name and address to be published, with the Editor's pesmissiun I will answer his queries relate ink to the Trades Council. When he asks what possessed the members of the Council to ' run 'Mr Flanagan, lam convinced he is net a regular reader of the " Examiner " reports, or he wend(' not be so ignorant of tbe subject he writes shout. Tis true that the Council " recommended " Mr Flana- gan's candidature, and if it would be interesting to know "why" I will inform "Mercury" on the conditiens previously named. In his cornpari• eons between the abilities of a Trade Unddriist, and a non Trade 'Unionist, your correspondent infers that the duties of elective auditor consist in being able to "add up a column of figures, or to do a simple multiplication sum" and immediately after he says, "The Council recommend a stove grinder to do a job that only a professional accountant could creditably petferin." Then he asks, "can consistency go much further "? Not satisfied with complaining, he suggests tha ; the Trades Council "if it can find no better justifi cation for its existence had better put its shutters up at once." Can "Murcia's," teach his Grandmother to suck eggs ? If so, he would be more profitably employed than giving advice to the Trades Council until be bag shown himself possessed of some degree of intelligence. In conclusion 'let me inform "Mercury" that the Trades Council have not selected Mr Edwin Plinston "because he was an insurance agent," but becamr. they consider him to be a fit person to become a member of the Board of Guardians. Why shouldn't an insurance agent be as fitted for that position as a publican, a Gr- iner, or any other class of tradesmen. Nay rather. I think insurance agents are more fitted, seeing that they more than any others, know the conditions and desires of the poorer working-class, who furnish the majority of inmates to the "Hou,e." "Mercury" acknowledges that insurance agents work hard for their living, but I find that among the retiring candidates whom "Mer cury" belauds, are several who do not work for their livirg, but live on the labeur of other men. My advice then to electors of Bewsey Ward is, if they want a can- didate who will be their friend, not only when they have money to spend, but when misfortune overtakes them. their duty is to work and vote for Mr Edwin Plinston the Trades Union Candidate. Thanking you in antici- pation, I remain, Faithfully yours, mrs- •ey • FRED. STOTT, . • Sec. to the Warrington Trades and Lab..ur Cauncil Sir,—The unexpected pleasure derived from reading the letter in y 'air last issue re the election of Guardians at first convulsed me with silent merriment, but upon reflection, the whole letter I can only regard as a remarkable tribute more indicative of a weak head

div.head: OPEN-AIR WORK.
div.p: OPEN-AIR WORK.

Of course. the regular work of the• National Council's missioners goes on as heretofore. But the next groat special Evangelistic enterprise is to bo a theatre and music-hall mission in the autumn of 1902. The Rev. F. C. Spurrggests in the religious weeklies that during the epmhlig summer open-Air campaigns sbouldbe organised As a matter-o'f-fact numbers of the Free Church Councils already engage in this work, and the Free Clo,rch chronicle, the official organ of the National Council, some time ago suggested that a Free Church Field Preaching Sunday should be organised.,

div.head: DR. PARKER AND OTHERS IN HYDE-PARK.
div.p: DR. PARKER AND OTHERS IN HYDE-PARK.

The Chronicle recalled the fact that Dr. Parker preached his first sermon in the open air, and continued: "If, it were announced that next Sunday afternoon he would peach in Hyde-park or on Hampstead-heath, we are confident that he would have nothing to com- plain of in the size and attention of his audience. It would b!!,rather a good idea, we think, to have a Free Church Field Preach- ing Sunday once or twice every summer. Take London, for illustration. There might be one central meeting place, say Fiyde- park. The Sunday afternoon, when Dr. Parker, Dr. Clifford, Mr. Price Hughes, Dr. Horton, Dr. Gibson, and a dozen other good Free Church preachers mount waggon pulpits in different parts of Hyde-park, and proclaim from thence the Gospel of Jesus Christ, will be a memorable and blessed occasion for London and the Churches. The plan strikes us as simple and feasible. An alternative proposal is to have a number of meeting-places all over London—Hampstead- heath, Finsbury-park, Peckham-rye, and so forth. But the concentrated effort would probably be the more impressive." The same sort of effort could easily be arranged in all the provincial towns and, indeed, all over the country.

div.head: KING AND THE FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE KING AND THE FREE CHURCHES.

His Majesty has received deputations and addresses from the National Free Church Council, the Congregational Union, the Baptist Union, the Dissenting Deputies, and other Nonconformist Associations. Dr. Guinness Rogers was a member of the Congregational deputation. The King, by a significant little gesture, showed that he remembered Dr. Rogers. As Dr. Rogers placed his hand on that of the King, his Majesty leaned slightly forward, and placed his ether hand on that of Dr. Rogers and gently pressed it. During the sittings of the Prince of Wales's Hospital Fund Committee, Dr. Rogers and the King—then Prince of Wales—were necessarily brought into personal relationship. One day a question of the representation of religious denomina tions on the Committee was under considers tion, and seemed likely to lead to prolonged discussion. But the Prince, rising from the ehair,.effectively closurecl discussion by saying, " Gentlemen ! Gentlemen! My friends Dr. Guinness Rogers and Bishop Creighton will settle this little matter between them in ten minutes." And they did.

div.head: NEW BISHOP OF LONDON.
div.p: THE NEW BISHOP OF LONDON.

Dr. Winnington Ingram is almost as much beloved by Free Churchmen as by members of his own Communion. And hi appointment as the successor of Dr. Creightr, is believed to be wise. As Head of-OxfOrd Hrtnse and later as Bishop of Stepney, Dr. Ingram was very popular with the East-enders. He has received mere than 3090 letters of congratula- tion on, his appointment—letters from 'bus 'drivers and conductors, from schoolboys and people of all classes. Dr. Ingram during the past three years has been obliged to spend a good deal of time in trams and 'buses, and underground railways. He is very popular as a preacher at St. Paul's Cathedral. His address to the returned C.l.V.'s was almost' perfect in substance; tone, and temper.
REV. lIVGH PRICE HUGHES, M.A.

During the meetings of the Free Church Council at Cardiff Mr. Hughes was staying with his brother at Barry, only a few miles off. The officials and prominent members. of' the Council visited him when the exigencies .of business permitted. Mr. Hughes is rapidly getting back his usual stock of ,health and vigour. He will not be long out of the fray.

div.head: PRINCIPAL FORSYTH.
div.p: PRINCIPAL FORSYTH.

Dr. Forsyth, of Cambridge, has accepted the principalship of ilackncy College, in.mtccession to the late Dr: Cave. He is ideally suited for the position, and it is.hoped that the lessened strain of work will leave him time for the writing of books. He may shortly attain to the position as a theologian occupied by Dr. Dale. Dr. Forsyth is a Scotsman, and there is still a pleasant trace of the Aberdonian accent in his speech.

div.p: rIHE EXAMIN-tEc, FRIDAY, MARCH 29, 1901

' than a's 'algisificant productidnloT t l feateT . Ife the local politiëai institutions had previously entertained - any 'fears regarding the " unwashed democracy " making a success ful eueroacbment into the &main of local poll tics, they need have no further anxiety on Cut score @irate Tour " well informed " correspondent " Mercury" has avowed himself their special champion and protec- tor. I observe that your am:able correseondent has required six peragraphs to shed the ligOt of his brilliant tellect on the stisve subjeet, bat I fail utterly to under- and Whst hisenstive C end be in wastine your mace, nd his stilt more vslueble time, that might with much rofit to himself have been better employed in uniiithing sense facts with -which- to-prop up hie most remarkable effort. Sir, the whole letter from top to bottom is singularly destitute of either fact or reapon, and-I prapose with your permission to review the pjeragraphe in which Lam directly interested, to les 'Oils that statement. In the first paragraph " Mere m!try ,says," A good deal has ben written of late in condemnation of the alleged compact between the poli- tical parties as affecting municipal contests " and also saye.l t,the charges were grossly false." - Nei* sir, after a series of letters appearing in 'your eort!eripondence column, bearing upon the subject. the last One was written by me, and WWI published in you/ issue .of January 1.9.-,h 1901. At this distant date it I!, difficult to imagine what your correspondent is driving at.. The "compact" was a fact, acknowledged by the chairmen of the Liberal and Conservative Clubs, and I have written nothing anent the sut.jsct that I have not the proof wherewith to :over the statements. It only remains for " Mercury" if he lace the instincts of a gentleman to point out where the falsehood is, or apolo- gize. In the next paragraph with " Mercury " I quite agree, but must point out that in his wisdom he has quite overlooked the fact that this paragraph has entirely cut the ground from under the feet of the one precedine it. The fourth paragraph is rather a personal one and was evidently conceived with the intention of giving me "le grand coupe," 19 e says," I shoulel like to as the members of the Trades and La our Council what possessed them to run Mr Flanagan for the elective auditorship on Trades Union lines. Can a Trsd Union- ist cla m that he can add up a celurnn of figures more quickly, or do a simple multiplication sum more accurately than a man who is not a 'Trades Unionist." With regard to the first sentence the Trades and L Lbour Council did not run Mr Flanagan at all, bus simply gave him their " moral support " being satisfied that be would have filled the position with credit to the general body of Trades Unionists in the borough. With respect to the next sentence, it has a distinct flavour of the nursery, and I treat it as men usually treat such meaningless prattle. Your "enlightened," corres- pondent, also goes on to insinuate with a delic cy that the most polished gentleman could not have excelled, that by contesting this election I was " Knobsticking." Sir, this impression is one of the vilest terms of reproach that ceuld be hurled at a workman, and I must say that I cannot regard it otherwise than as a delibArate insult, and especially when delivered from behind the bulwarks of a nom de plume. It makes the person off ring it far too contemptible to be worthy of any further attention on th p In conclusion let me remark, that, " Mercury" eve. dently judges " personal fitness and ability," by the money, or social standard. Will " Mercury " explain upon whet grounds he bases his opinion, that Trades Unionists, or workmen generally. when eleoted by those who know and understand them best, should lack the intelligence necessary for local administration. One fact is quite evident," Mercury " entertains no kindly feelings towards Trade Unionises. I wonder why P Lt me give" Mercury "a tittle advice, in a friendly way : Cultivate veracity and sweetness of disposition, before again writing to the Press. It is preferable to " ignor- ance at once comprehensive and astounding." Thaek- ing you in anticipation, I am yours respectfully. MARTIN FLANAGAN. ----- Warrington Guardians and the Religion of Officials. Sirs—l desire to thank the Rev 3 Ynnge for the courteous and temperate tone of his criticism on a recent ruling by me as Chairman of the Board of Guardians. From the concluding sentences of his letter I infer that he suspects me of permitting questions to be put to candidates for emploement at the Union Workhouse with the purpose f excluding some of them on religious grounds., May I most em- phatically say that the Guardians of the Warrington Union have given no occasion for even the shadow of a suspiction that they are influenced by reactionary motiies or are in any way ohn xious to the charges of religious intolerance ? Amongst the hundreds of sick and of aged poor under their care are peesons of many denominations and the Guardians are by law compelled to keep a register of the creed to which eaco inmate of the Workhouse belongs. They strive, as far as practicable, to provide that eaeh inmate shall have facilities for worship aecnrding to his belief. A little reflection en the di ffieulties 'of managing family of about 400, many of them much enfeebled by age or disease, will conviece any fair-minded person that the provision of such religious essisAnce can be best effected with a mixed staff. This the Guardians have kept in view, and have accordingly amongst their resident officials, Roman Catholics, Protestant Noncan- formists and members of the EstaleiLhed Church. My colleagues have tried to deal with the religious difficulty in the most tolerant and sympathetic spirit. and I think that our efforts have been crowned with success. With the general proposition that " the days of religions tests are ever "I cordially agree ; but in forming an opinion on the fitness of a person to become a resident official in such an ir stitution as the Warrington Workhouse one factor must be that person's religion ; ner can I conceive any honest man or woman being ashamed to say to what religious body be or she belongs. To elaborate -be arguments in defence of my ruling would involve too great a trespass on your space; let it suffice to say that my precedure was legally un- assailable, morally justifiable, and practically useful Though we may not FPO eye to eye in this matter, my reverend friends, Messrs Riddette and Yonee, will scarcely dispute toy claim to be as sineere a " lover of religious liberty " as either ot them —Yours. am_ AL?. 3 JOLLEY, Marihhonse lane, March 23rd, 1901.

INDIGESTION CURED.

LI his observations upon the estimates and precedure of the Council for the ensuing half-year the Clerk said it was satisfactory to find after careful consideration of the Council's funds, and after consultation with the Surveyor that the prospect held out by the Assistant Clerk, at the last Council meethag, of the Council's pre- vious decision to add one penny to the call upon town- ships for each of the nex- two half yeare to admit of payment of the two instalments contracted to be paid by the Council in the two half years for the new steam roller and scarifier, miebt be acted upon and that the calls [or health, sanitery,rcerd, and ether purposes might be limited to the corresponding call, of sixpence, as made at the same period of 1900. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
2dAROII 29th, 1901.
The American Canal Negotiations.
THE temperate and
forci'3le despatch in

which Lord LANSnowNE handles the amendments made to the Hay- -I)euecefote Treaty will meet with general ap- PruYal• He was, of course, compelled to expound the principles of the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty of 18'50,and to deal seriously with each of the amend- made by the American Senate. Their Reneral object, and the circumstances under which they Were made, form no part of Lord LANs- )YlN's's despatch. He treats the whole subjeet 441, it 4 international aspect, and not as an ebulli- ""es of anti-British politics. He was bound to do tha3, and to write as if the gravity of the matter 7"e as impressive to the authors of the amend- as it seems to us on this side of the Atlantic. c' Paints out that, as far as the British Govern- , °lit Was concerned, " there was no desire to pro- modification of that Convention "—i.e., the '1437t0n-Bulwer Treaty. We entered upon the nlgotiations to oblige the American Governmen , 44(1 there was an assurance from the PRESIDENT •t he had "no intention whatever of ignoring the layton-Bulwer Convention, and that he would 'Y dly observe the treaty stipulations." The Clayte-Bulwer Treaty sets forth that "The Govern- esents of Great Britain and the United States ilarebY declare that neither the one nor the other Will ever obtain o; maintain for itself any exclusive rentroi over the said canal, agreeing that neither will ever erect or maintain any fortifications cone- 43ncling the same or in the vicinity thereof." The l'aendinents to the Hay-Pauncefote Convention give to the United States Government the •i)le right to interfere with the Nicaraguan CAnal 'll time of war or apprehended war, and, as L LeNspowmt says, "while other Powers with a clear 9°Aseience disregard any of the restrictions itzt- 'l°Becl by the Convention, Great Britain alone, in yte ot her enormous possessions on the American U9ritinent, in spite of the extent of her Australa- Sian Colonies, and her interests in the East. would be absolutely precluded from resorting to any such action, or from taking measures to secure her in- terests in or near the eanal." That is, the changes *eve not suggested to safeguard the joint interests the individual interests of the two countries alit to hamper and injure Great Britain. The '4lthers of the amendments designed to accomplish t/145e things, and hence the agreement has been ~'atered to lapse. We are now exactly as we were .'sfore, The Clayton-Bulwer Convention is sttict 'sternational law, and it cannot be abrogated by mutual consent. The threat that if In not agree to the amendments the Treaty of R:CI should be abandoaed we can afford to disre- 0. It is not made by the Government of the t'ki States, and were it so made it would be a frie lon of international law and a distinctly ip;ritilY no- act. As has been said before, in dealing th the subject, the majority in the Senate was of politicians animated by different aims. tna of its members were adverse to the making Canal at all because they were influenced by eat American railway interests, and a few were Itile to this country. The whole subject has 3°,l3seu loft open, and it cannot be said that it , pee treated with any lack of courtesy,dignity t'' legility upon our part. We have done our to meet American desires, and we can now 11 to wait until more reasonable counsels pre- ”eil • le the American Senate.

P"chesShor THE idea that Parlia- ". t Long and. mentary time is consumed Of, by long speeches, is one ''ur current delusions. Speeches are shorter th,,,„ they used to be when oratory was cultivated, witintstions were common, and abstract themes ~lare constantly enlarged upon by rising young au fresh from the University who wanted to • Metz. mark in the House of Commons. The °t long speeches and long debates are behind '4O Perhaps they will not return until we have large measure upon which much will require trk khe Bald. Obstruction does not consist in 'lv 134 1"g apeechee, and it will not be cured by 'l,4' Provision of a tirae-limit for ordinary mem- time-limit implies that many persons want 1,„ 11'1411) and that time is so precious that it must etlt uP into sed it Portions. But if a timo-limit be Will oni need a number of persons to agree

to occupy the allotted time to consume more time than ever. A new form of obstruction will be introduced of which the acute will soon learn how to avail themselves. If the time-limit be twenty minutes, three speeches an hour have only to be arranged by theobstructives, and twenty persons can with ease occupy between them some six hours and forty minutes. A band of sixty or seventy members would soon learn to adapt themselves to any rule of this kind, and the existence of the rule would encourage and warrant speaking to that length. The five, ten, or fifteen minutes speaker would become a rarity. The evil in Par- liament is not that a few men speak far a long time, but that they speak very frequently and upon every variety of subject. No rule would be tolerated which limited their right to speak to a few occasions, and so reformers think they are on safe ground in atiizing a time-limit to all persons except Ministers and ex-Ministers. The rule would not work well, and it would not cure any existing evil. The House of Commons contains many able men whose views are worth listening to, and some men who are amusing and at times loqqacious. At present there is no rule to reduce the one order of member to the level of the other. A time-limit would do it, and therefore it is ob- jectioanble. The House of Commons is too large for any rapid discharge of duty, and a rapid discharge is undesirable,and may easily become mischievous. Free speech has its penalties, and we must be con- tent to pay them. Ministers would be despots if every member was bound by rule and order in everything he said and did, and his liberty of speech were curtailed. Just now we have in power Ministers who dislike criticism, but who were talkative and verbose enough when in Opposition; and we must resist, in the public in- terest, their efforts to obtain power to slip business through as if talk were an offence and objection were unpatriotic and treasonable. The outcry against talk and obstruction is often mere vexa- tion, and no doubt some supporters of the existing Government have sufficient to create vexation in their minds as to the bungling way in which busi- ness has been managed, and may be glad of an opportunity of charging the mismanagement on others. The Irish members have taken an active part in recent Parliamentary discussions, but they have every right to do so under the Constitution, and the Unionists cannot have the union without its inconveniences. As Mr Redmond has frankly said more than once, Irishmen would much rather attend to their own business at home; but they are constitutionally summoned to London, and if we will not make terms with them we shall have to put up with their frequent speeches. The Im- perialists should welcome the candid views of Ireland about Imperial affairs, because their absence from Westminster used to be grandly ob- jected to as "Imperial disintegration."

People are still complaining bitterly of being pnif4oned by the famous or infamous " Thelwall Nuisance," which has engaged the attention of the Runcorn Rural Council for so many months. Medical officers have reported on the nuisance, deputations have inspected it, and at present it is in charge of the Local Government Board, whose methods may be sure but they are undeniably slow. This week two letters full of grievous com- plaint from residents of "ye anciente citye of Thal- wall " were read before the Runcora authority an 1 I both seem to be bona fide lamentations. Fears are entertained that the condition of affairs will be much worse when the hot weather comes—if it is ever coming—and no doubt they will unless adequate remedial measures are promptly taken. I It does not seem quite clear yet whether it is sewage or the Tannery effluent which is primarily blameable for the foul smells which undoubtedly permeate the atmoqphere of this otherwise pleasant rural locality. Possibly the point will be finally cleared in the near future. At any rate the Run- corn Councillors are treating the complaints with more seriousness than formerly, and in the mean- time they have decided to jog the memory of the Local Government Board.

The Easter holidays fall too early in the year for the tourist agencies and the railway' companies to , be able to:make much profit out of the break in the 'routine of business, but the vast number of adver- tisements on the subject point to Easter as .the time for the beginning of tours and excursions. There are only two continental cities which appeal to the British public at this season—they are, of course,Paris and Rome. But it is hardly passible to sit in the open in Paris at this time of the year; and, although there is no period so good for sight- seeing, the visitor who returns frequently to the French capital must prefer a little later date. For a first impression of Rome, however, there are no moments so appropriate as when the religious ceremonials lend their fullest contrast to the wealth of ancient traditions with which the buildings are store 4. There is a familiar phrase which describes Brussels as a miniature Paris, but in many ways it is singularly disappointing. It has one good quarter; but its restaurants and cafés, which afford so correct an index to the life of a people, are, generally speak- ing, much inferior to those either of Patis or Vienna. The best thing that can be said about Brussels is that the hotel tariffs are reasonable, and it is the nearest place that affords any toter- able reflection of Continental manners. The question may very well be asked, however, why people with only ten days' or a fortnight of spare time should go abroad. This sea-girt island can offer the best of tonics, under widely different con• damns of climate; according as one goes east, west, north, or south. And then, there are the hydropatinc establishments, whose only defect is that they aro so near. If only they were a few hundred miles off, instead of in the midst of Eng- land, they would gathAr twice as many patrons.

A music al critic in one of the weeklies, who has been girding at the ridiculous libretti of peer poet Laureate Nahum Tate, would, perhaps, have been more profitably employed in calling attention to the verbal rubbish with which so many of our best musicians are content. No doubt the libretto of " Dido and iEneas " contains surpassing gems of the unconsciously comic order. For instance : "Thus on the fatal banks of Nile, Weeps the deceit- ful crocodile," is a couplet which fairly deserves immortality, and there are others almost equally amusing, such ns "Our plot has took, the Queen's forsook." Could not these, however, be matched, or almost so, from among the latest operas, whether the libretti were originally in English, or affect to be translations from the German or the Italian? The fact is, the word has gone forth in musical circles that any trash will do for setting to music; and, indeed, the view it not .without some justification,seeing how many songs in which " dove " rhymes with " love " and " heart with " part " have sold of late years in their thousands. It is said sometimes that musicians have endless trouble with their libretto writers,and that modern poets will not compose verses of the directneis and simplicity which musical setting demands. A juster view of the position is that much of the weakness and the esoteric character of modern verse is due to its divorce from the art with which poetry was once invariably joined—a separation which, it is clear, is not without disastrous effect also on the other member of the dissolved union.

During the week-end the people: of this country will have to devote:some portion of their spare time to satisfying the curiosity of the census enumerators, and elucidating the somewhat com- plax. sheet of questions which has been issued to them. There is always a good deal of fun to be got out of" taking the census," and within the n.,Nt few weeks the Press will be embellished with

ca-nsus yarns of the usual remarkable typo, Som people cannot answer a straight question in a straight fashion, and others won't, so th4t it is not easy for the enumerators to obtain all the information they require. They require such a lot, too. After it has been decided—by right of conquest, survival of the fittest, or mutual agree- ment—who is the head of the family, that incb- vidual has to take up his pen and com- mence to record. What he has to record we will leave the paper to explain, in the main. But we might just impress on the proud head of the family, that after he has written down the name of John Henry, as his oldest son, he must carefully state the sex of the said John Henry, as the census people are very particular about this matter. Likewise must he deal with " Sar' Ann?' and all the other boys and girls who have any claim to a sex at all. Among other things it is also necessary to state who is lunatic, imbecile, or feeble-minded. The delicacy of the subject has not to be considered for a moment. If the" head" thinks John Henry imbecile and " Sar' Ann" [ feeble-minded he must say so without fear or favour. In regard to himself he should be equally candid,and if in doubt as to which or any category he comes under, consult his best friend. With proper attention paid to these, among other pre- cautions, we think the papers should be filled up withoutiany possibility of error and in such a man- ner as will unfeignedly delight the enumerators.

Apropos of the division on the Sale of Drink to Children's Bill last week, we notice that the name of Mr Pierpoint appears amongst the "noes." This gentleman, we presume, is the distinguished individual whom many in Warring- ton are pleased to call "our member." We should like to know whether Mr Pierpoint believed he was representing the best interests of Warrington and reflecting the opinions of the majority of his constituents, when he voted against this simple measure of protection for the children of the coun- try. Mr Pierpoint at least earned distinction, for out of 54 L Incashire and Cheshire M.P.' s who took part in the division there were only Mr R Pier- point, Colonel W H Walker, and Sir J Fergusson who voted against the Bill.

To this end, and in order that each man may obtain special training in what, are called " proper .war duties,' Volun- teer camps will be held between May let and Sep- tember 30th, at places suitably situated and pro- vided, according to the arm of the service. div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

It is important, as well as interesting, to observe that throughout the provincesfas well as in London, steps are being taken to erect worthy and enduring memorials of Queen Victoria and her great reign Ceatain of the ci.' ies and towns have decided to support the national scheme inaugurated at a meet- ing in London on Tuesday; while many have de- termined to divide theie financial suppor between local mementos and the central one; and others have agreed upon the local memorial only. New- castle-on-Tyne has decided to stand in with the Mansion House scheme. Manchester will erect a bronze statue of her late Majesty, but it is worthy of note that not a few towns of importance have come to the conclusion that it would be b4ter to complete or to amplify existi 'I; institutions than to embark on new undertakina. Leicester proposes to establish a Convalescent Home and to add a new wing to the Hospital. Bournemouth is to found a Victorian bed in the exi,ting Convalescent Home, besides forward,ng the endowment of other medi- cal charities; while Blackburn is raising £lO,OOO for a statue, and the endowment of a Disbri ,t Nursing Fund. Bolton will endow a Victorian wing in the local Hospital. These decisions are, of course, not without interest and use to other places where the Victorian memorial movemeot has not yets been begun or defined, so far as the general public are concerned. They will, at least, s.owe the purpose of giving hints and suggestions to the latter.

During the last four or five days experts and prophets have reached the stage at which their opinions as to the results of to-day's Great Boat Race had begun to crystallise, and although in boat races, as in every other athletic contest, the element of chance is always more or less a factor, it seems to be held that th + Oxford crew will this morning have the advantage. The event cvi I be decided between ten and eleven 1 o'clock The practice made by the Cambridge men has been described as faulty in several respects,and they have been declared to be lacking in cohesion. The training within the last day or two may have helped to modify this fault,for otherwise they are a powerful body of oarsmen. The Oxford crew is composed of m...n d-cidedly above the average, and trials over the full course have revealed their strength If there is one thing the Eaglishman dislik-s at a boat race it is a "process,on," and even the most ardent friends of Oxford will wish that the Cantabs may be able to give th jr opponents all possible trouble in scor ng a victory.

The rumour is revived that Sir Michael Hicks- Beach will put a halfpenny per pound upon sugar. This being he case, the consumers have mainl to consider whether such a tax would be conducive to the financial welfare of the buyer all round. The imposition of a tat upon beet sugar will tend t) cripple the production of all those articles in which sugar is an ingredient. Cocoa, jam, sweets, biscuits, and other articles of daily consumption will all be enhanced in price. The householder will also have to pay dearer for the sugar he uses in the ordinary course. Therefore, the higher price of sugar that must necessarily ensue on the embarr -sment of the beet sugar imports will touch the pocket of the consumer at many points.

Boards of Guardians may feel pleased to have the assurance of one of the Poor-law Inspectors that the Workhouse dietary need not he so expensive as some of them have imagined. According to what nr Preston Thomas has said, sme of the Boards have discussed and denounce I the new regulations without taking particular pains to find out what they really are. With a choice of sixty-three dinners, and a range f comlete dietaries costing anything from two shillings to four shillings per head per week, guardians must have little to com- plain of as regards any restriction of choice, or be- ing olaliged to incur unreasonable expe tse. All that the order seems to require, after all, is that a Board of Guardians should fix one the numerous dietary scales and carry i out. If they find it unsuitable,they may try anothe and may thus go through all the ran,ze of variations; or give the Workhouse inmve, a different menu now and again, or on the other hand adhere to the one they first select: There cannot. aisuredly, be much to compl.ain of in this. S)me Boards,especially in rural districti, have been c incerned at the thought that all milk had to be new, or raw milk. But this is net so, and where buttermilk is aimed scald milk may be used if preferred.

it is a week since the sun entered Aries; so that however inclement the weather has been, we must assume technic;lly that spring is with us an,l sum- mer on the way. Fortunitely, everyone is not ohl.ged to act accordingly. So much for the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern, people are at tnis time preparing for the rig 'Lire of winter,and are looking forward thereto. ILnce the war-office the other day, as if on set purposes to mark these differences, issued, simultaueothly and independeurly, a sutnmer programme for the home training of the Volunteer forces, under the new army scheme and a list of sugges- tions as to the supply of the winter com- forts for our troops in South Africa. In the latt connection, there can be no doubt that from all parts of the provinces the response to the ' appeal just made by Lord Kitchener for supplies of comforts for the troops in the coming winter will be hearty and cheerful. At this time last year, the war, though it hai been in progress some mon-hs, was invested with a certain air of novelty for most people, and was accompanied by stirring and start- ling, and even alarming incidents, which struck the public mind sharply. The novelty has now worn away, and with it may have gone some of the enthusiasm, but just as the com- forts of men engaged in last winter's campaign were provided, it is hoped and eirp,.e'sed they will be provided this year. The re- jpmion of the peace overtures by Botha has made it certain that the larger part, if not the whol-, of the army there will have to serve through a second winter.

Provincial volunteers would do well to note that the directions just issued from the War Office are intended for the guidance and information of men belonging to the corps selected for inclusion in one or other of the six Army Corps into which the military forces are to be divided. It is needless to say that the new plan will demand from the Volun- teers sacrifices even more substantial than those which the country has hitherto, of course gratefully

div.head: CENSUS.
div.p: THE CENSUS.
[ Examiner" Special.]

On Sunday night, a census paper will he in the hands of every responsible householder throughout the whole of England and Wale., Scotlan4 and Inland, and within a month of to-day we shall know, not only facts about the population of these islands, but also many interesting details about the employment of the people. Toe history of the " census," is not by any meens shrouded in mystery. But the disaster which accompanied the census" of King David, described id I. Chronicles !xi., and spoken of as : " David's sin in numbering the people; whereupon seventy thousand are destroyed by pestilence," if it were repeated would deter even our Registrar General and his vast army of enumerators from venturing upon the task. However, the census of the present day, being entirely for a different purpose to that of King David's, can be accomplished with impunity. The origin of the system, is, no doubt, traceable to the Romans ; who having advanced along the line of civilisation and enlightenment I perhaps as far as any nation, found it a political necessity. It was introduced by King Servius Tallius, B.C. 577; and under the system all Romm citizens were obliged to .report the amount of their property, the number of their children, values, &c., under penalty of losing their property and their liberty. A. for ourselves,the numbering of the population of Great Britian and Ireland was appointed to be taken every tenth year by Act 41, George 111., cApt. 15 (December 1800), and consequently the first Census was taken in 1801, and has been repeated every tenth year since. Naturally, each recurring census has been rendered more complete,and at the present time elicits a vast amount of valuable in- formation.

div.head: CRNSTIS PAPERS._
div.p: THE CRNSTIS PAPERS._

These have, n-o—do-uht, been distribmed by now. The documents are supposed to be filled by the " head-of-the-family," but in thousands of homes unfortunately the work will have to be delegated to others, because of the inability of the" head 'to read and write. Naturally the number of such cases will be much smaller than was the case when the Census was taken ten years sgo,but it is lamentable that the country has still in its midst a vast army of uneducated people. This year, however, the Registrar General has sought the aid of children, a step the wis- dom of which everyone will readily agree with and for some days past the chilciren of our elementary ,chools have been engaged filling up imaginary census papers, so that, in the case of need, they will be in a position to help their parents to fill up the " documents" properly. THE PAPERE MUST BE FILLED.

Householders will do well to bear in mind that the filling of the census paper is obligatory. There is no escape from the duty, and furnishing false in- formation is punishable and entails a pemalty not exceeding] Li. Apart from any penalty every inhabitant will readily recognise it is his plain duty to give every detail askad for in order ' that the returns may be as exhaustively correct as possible. Name. age, birthplace, condition, and oc- cupation of every person sleeping in the house on the night of March 30th are to be set down on the cenQus paper, and the clearer the details are writen th 3 better for all concerned.

div.head: 'WHAT TO BEAR IN MIND.
div.p: 'WHAT TO BEAR IN MIND.

Each schedule bears full instructions and exam- ples for the guidance of persona whose duty it is to till up the paper, and in case of doubt he or she may call in a neighbour or obtain the assistance of the enumerator. The column in the census paper describing the profession or occupation of the people to be enumerated may cause confusion to some. There are three classes—one, persons who are employers; another, those who are workers; and a third, those who work "on their own," but who do:not employ assir..ants. This latter class would Include many small shopkeepers who conduet I their own businesses without help, and very likely a few professional men. Pall details are required of the character of employment in which workers are engaged. "Shop assistant," for instance,is not sufficient. It is absolutely necessary to indicate the nature of the calling—milliner's assistant, grocer's assistant, chemist's assistant, and so on. An engin- eer will be obliged to state "civil," ‘` mechanical," " mining," or" electrical," as the case may be. And it will not be anflicient for a" weaver" to say be is " weever," lie must state "cotton weaver," and other textile operatives must also make it clear 38 to 'whether it is wool, silk, cotton, or what particu- lar material they are industrially engaged upon. An " hotel porter" is a different person from a " railway porter" or a "traveller's porter,' and all these different grades of employ- ment must be particularised. The term "gentle- man "is happily not recognised by the census paper, and the individual who has laid aside the cases of lnisiness,tsmmerce and profession, and is accounted a " gentleman " in the popular sense is riluir,id for the purposes of the return to state the particular occupation he followed before he crysta- lised, as " retired pork-butcher," " retired solicitor" &c. As for the idler, that individual who never hes figured in the "Nation's Workshop," the entry "living on own means " is to be made by him, but gentleman, Esq., &c., are forbidden. The census papers will therefore disclose the interesting fact that there are no gentlemen in the United King- dom. RUNCORN RIGISTRATION DISTRICT.
