OLD FOLKS' PRZAT.

The annual treat to the old folks of Runcorn is to be given on Wednesday, April 10th, 1901, in the Public Hall. In our advertising columns thera appears an appeal for donations, which we hope will be handsomely responded to,

div.head: r NEW OEMS AT DITTON.
div.p: r NEW OEMS AT DITTON.

It is rumoured that Messrs. J. Midwood and Sons have acquired a lease of land for new works at Ditton. One acre has been acquired with the option of taking an additional four acres. The works are for the treatment of spent oxide. As the land has already been measured out it is presumed that the erection of the 'works are to be commenced at once,
DEATH FROM _BLOOD POISONING AT WIDNES

The Widnes police report the death of a man named David Raw, aged 64 years, who resided at 13, Frederick-street. The deceased had not been in good health for about six months, but has been able to follow his employment at the Tharsis Copper Works. On Thursday, the 28th ult., he fell over a whrelbarrow and scratched hieing. Blood poison- ing set in, and he died at 940 on Friday night. HOPE HALL, RUNCORN. At the P S E held on Saturday the programme was funished by Mr Byfleld's concert party. There was a good attendance.S.ings were given by Messrs T Dutton,J Baxley, Misses Shaw, Inman, Gibson, and Mrs Gatley ; recitations by Mr T Inman, and Miss Sanders, and gramaphone selections by Mr Byfield. The various items made up a capital en- ' tertaintnent, and at times the audience were quite enthusiastic wish their applause. INQUEST AT RUNCORN. On Tharsday, sir R Dobson, the coroner, held an inquest on the body of Robert McGuffy, 'on-ttreet, labourer, who died on Tuesday. Dr Robinson gave a certificate that the primary cause of death was amputation of the arm followed by septic pneumonia; The allegation was that the de- ceased had had a fall at Wiggs Works, whic'shad 80 injured his arm that the limb had to be amputated.--Mr George Wainwright, manager of the copper department, at Old Quay Works said that deceased never complained of having any accident at the works. Had he met with an acci- dent at the works be would have received half pay, which was a strong inducement to the men to re- port the most trivial accidents. The deceased never made any report. The jury returned a verdict of death from septic pneumonia. ELECTION OF GUARDIANS FOR WIDNES. The election for the vacancy on the Prescot Board of Guardians caused by the retirement of Alderman Wareing took place on Monday in the West Bank Ward at Widnes. Councillor T Smith, grocer, and W J Trevorrow, ironmonger, were the candidates, and the result was declared as follows by Mr T Craik, deputy town clerk, the same night. Smith, 344, Trevorrow, 101. Majority, 243. The result was listened to by a large crowd, but there was no ap- parent excitement. Mr Smith and Mr Trevorrow afterwards thanked their supporters. DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORN/AN. Another old Runcorrian has just passed away in the person of Miss Martha Simeon, of Brunswick- street. The deceased lady had been the victim of a painful malady for some few months past, and des- Oite the unremitting attention of Dr. Robinson she gradually sank and died on Saturday morning The deceased was deeply attached to the Parish Church, and besides being a regular attendant at the services she did what she could to farther the parochial work in the capacity of district visitor. Among others she took a deep interest in the work of the Local Committee assoniated with the Chester Rescue Home for Women Far many years she had carried on a private school for young ladies. She was highly respected in the town, and much sym- pathylis felt for the members of th family in their bereavement. STE.ERT ACCIDENT AT WIDNES —WARRINGTON Finm's HORSE KILLED.

About six o'clock on Friday night a shocking street accident occurred in Waterloo-road, whish resulted in the death of a horse belonging to Messrs Bennett and Sons, confectioners, Derby House, Lovely-lane, Warrington. It appears that a lai in the employ of the firm was in charge of the cart, and in turning pretty sharply round the bend lead- ing from Victoria-road to Waterloo-road he collided with considerable force with a light cart belonging to John Hall.greengrocer and fishmonger,Waterloo- road, Widnes. One of the shafts of the latter vehicle was, unfortunately, driven with great force into the breast of the animal bslonging to Messrs Bennett and Sons, and, breaking off short, killed it instantly. It lay on the roadside for at least an hour, causing a great crowd of people to assemble. Eventually Mr R Allan, horse slaughterer, removed the body. • _ _

MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. Last Friday the weekly concert at the Seaman's Institute was given by the Misses Hayes' party of Prodsharn. There Was only a moderate attendance. ldrJ K Digges took the chair,and Miss V Hayes gave the opening selection "Roberts to the front," on the pianoforte. The children performed a Japanese fan drill with commendable precision, which called forth loud applause. The recitation, "Flo's letter," was rendered by a child, and Mies Harrison was heard to advantage in "Came back to Erin." The ' song and chorus, "Silly Fish," was interpreted by the children. Miss Hayes gave a delightful selection on the zither, and tbe juveniles were soh loudly epplauded for a Scotch dance, executed inn most lamming manner. "Play up," by the ladies con. chided the first portion et the programme. The second part was introduced by a spirited rendering of " Soldiers in the Park," by the troupe. The recitation, "Going on an errand," in the hands of one of the.children,was received with much favour. Other items which went to make up a good pro- gramme were" Daddy," by Miss Clarke; tte chorus. " .Che New Baby," by the juveniles ; "Going to Market," by Miss Edwards; "Cock Robin," by the Children; and an amusing recital of troubles of the "Inventw's Wife." The ladies wound up the enter- tainment with a song and chorus in gold style. A vote of thanks was accorled to the Misses Hayes and party and to Mr Digges for presiding, and the meeting closed with the National Anthem. The accompanists were the Misses Higson and Hayes

The monthly meeting was held on Friday evening in the Court Room, Mr C E Linaker presiding.—The Clerk reported that the revenue from the water rents during the past year amounted to £584 8s ld, whilst the expenses had exceeded that sum by 2s, which was considered very satisfactory.—The 911 a) of £25 was voted to Mr Ashton for services ren- dered as clerk during the past year. "Tax AGE 'WE LIVIC IN" Will form the stoject of a lecture to be delivered by the Rev Alfred Wells, (super- intendent of the Wesleyan Circuit), at the Biunswick School, on Monday, April Ist, in connection with the Runcorn Free Church. The small ,charges of 01 and 31 will be made for ad- mission, and the lecture will commence at 8 o'clock, the doors being open at 7.30. A capital opportunity is afforded, and should be availed of, both to hear a good lecture and aid a good cause. CONFIRMA.TION SERVICE.

On Tuesday evening Dr Jayne, Biahop of Chester held a confirmation service at Runcorn Parish Church. There was a good congregation. Candi- dates for confirmation were presented as under: Parish Church (including St Michael's and Weaton) males 69, females 61 ; Holy Trinity, males 19, females 5; Halton, males 5, females 7; Weston Point, males 3, females 5; St James Latchford, 2 females: total 96 males and 80 females. His lord- ship delivered the Customary addresses which were void of public interest.

RUNCORN WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. The annual meeting of the above wai held on Monday, March 25th, when the following ladies were elected to serve for the ensuing year :—Presi- dent, Mrs Harry Baker; vice-presidents, Mrs R Morris, Mrs Reynolds, and Mrs Simkin ; treasurer, Mrs Wilton ; secretary, Mrs Cameron ; assistant secretary, Miss Carter; and an Executive Commit- tee of 15 ladies. The report showed an increase of eight members during the year. After the rep3rt end balance sheet had been read and confirmed, Mrs Sprunt, late secretary of the Port Sunlight Branch of tho N.B.W.T A., pave a short address, Tim c RASTER HOLIDAYS Naturally, the holiriay maker will be on the look out for somewhere to go to during Eastertide. With- out going far afield, he will find much to amuse and relax himself or hersblf at the Mersey View I Picnic grounds, Frodsham, The enterprising wattagereas Mrs Parker noose, has with her usual good taste had the whole of the pleasure grounds and building overhauled On Good Friday,the Frod- sham Volunteer Band will play for dancing ;on ISaturday Mr T Knight's celebrated Quadrille Band will bs in attendanc) ; and on the Bank Holiday (Monday), the Frodsham Volunteer Band will be agar!' in attendance, For other particulars see ad- vertisemen t.

FRODSHAM PETTY SESSIONS. Messrs A Thomas and George C Taylor were the presiding magistrates at Frodsham Sessions on Thursday. J Dykes was granted temporary auth- ority to sell at the Bridge Inn, lately occupied by Mr James Worrall.—Ten Frodsham youths for , loitering on the footpath at Overton were ordered to pay di 6.1 costs each.—George Smith, labourer,Frod- sham, and Richard Relsby. of Frodsham Lordship, were each fined 5s f,-,r drunkenness and disorderly conduct.—Andrew Hutchinson, auctioneer, Prod- sham, and William Boosey, nurseryman, Middle- wich,for obstructing the footpath in Nain-street,by holding a sale of fruit trees were ordered to pay 10s 6d. and 91 6d respectively, the costs of the action.

RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL, A special meeting of this Connell was held on Tuesday night fur the purpose of passing accounts to close the financial year. Mr W Handley, JP, presided, and there were present—Messrs Grice, Kirkham, Walton, Lightburn, lmison, Bisbrown, Salkeld, Jones and Dean,with F A. Lake (law clerk) and E Marshall (secretary). On the proposition of lmison, seconded by Mr Salkold, cheques were drawn amounting to ..£3 740 10s sd. The Chairman explained that r. great proportion of thia sum was transfers to different funds It was also resolved, on the proposition of Mr Indison, seconded by Mr Dean, that applicatfon be made to the Local Government Board for sanction of an account of .£7B for the purchase of a herse, and an account of £52 10 for the purchase of an ambulance cart CYCLE ACCIDENT. On Tuesday shortly after dinner Mr Byrne, wine and spirit merchant of Runcorn, Widnes and St. Helens, met with a Serious accident at Weston Mr Byrne attempted to ride his cycle down the steep road which leads to Weston Chemical Works.l lie lost control of the manine and jumped off, but his foot caught a p-.dal and he was flung to the ground with great violence. He was carried into the laboratory at the works where first aid was rendered. He was then taken in a cab to Runcorn railway station ' where Dr McDougall bandaged his wounds. He was taken home by the firs, available train, Mr Green of the laboratmry staff kindly accompanying him. Besides suffering a severe shock Mr Byrne's head and face were very badly cut and bruised, his left arm was dislocated and several of , his ribs were damaged. The bicycle sustained little or no damage.

div.head: ---•••---. THE HEALTH OF-RUNCORN.
div.p: ---•••---. THE HEALTH OF-RUNCORN.

For thebenefit of our readers we publish the following digest of Dr McDopieall'e annual report of the Health of the District. In 1900 there were 97 ootifievione of In- fectious disease, embracing 95 cases. 'Compared with the three previous years the numbers of notifications show a decrease of 182,212 and 188 respectively. Scar- let fever was responeible for nine notifications, as against 12 in 1899. The msjerity of the cases were im- ported. Enteric fever accounted for 41 notifications, which embraced 38 oases. Of typhoid fever there were twelve notific ttione, as compared with 24 in 1899, and of erysipelas 17 notifications, as compared with 11 in the preceding year. Tee number of emes of diphtheria notified was 18, as cnmp sr d with 99 in 1899 and 222 in 1898. Dr McDougall says it is gratifying to find that this formidable disease has ceased to have an epidemic character, but he fears that there is every probability of the disease making its appearance in the sporadic form The total number of deatta registered during the year was 354, as compared with 290 in 1899, and 331 in 1898. One hundred and one of these deaths were those of infants. The death-rate is equal to 181 per thousand of ' the estimated population, which, the Medical Officer says, for an industrial centre, is fairly, if not eminently sttiefactory. The improvements of the year bear a eatis- factory ratio to past years, and have a permanent value of their own. The authority has every reason to be satisfied with the highly favourable sanitary condition the town is eradually getting into, and its general immenicy from the zymotic claim of diploma. The num- ber of births registered during the year was 553, a decrease of 24 as compared with 1899. The number of births in ereese of deaths was 199. The birth-rate was equal to 28-3 per thousand of the estimated population. In concluding his report Dr McDougall calls the atten- tion of tho authority to the noceneity of a more regular administ,ation of the Food and Drugs Act. The report of the Sanitary inspnctor (Mr James Perci- val) states that during the past rear 309 nuisances were ditcovered and 293 were abated. The supervision of mi'kehope and coweheds has been regular, and only in •wo instances was there any cause for complaint. The supervision of registered common lodging-houses has also been regular, and only in one instance was there cause for complaint.

div.head: . RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: . RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A _CORRESPONDENT.]

Trade prospects just ac. present are not of the rosiest hue, and numbers of workingmen have been stopped temporarily al. mlre than one ot our large establishments. In the shipping deparanents too, there does not appear to be very much Clil for labour, and the "layby" and dicks are considered to be doing well when all the "regulars" have their ' hands occupied. The conditions of things, let us hope, are likely to change for the better alter the holidays.

In days of yore we were wont to associate Vestry Meetings, end "the story of the parish pump" witk Eastertide. Now, however, the Parish Council and Pariah Meeting largely detract from the Vestry as. semblies, and cue business of the latter is generally but of a formal ecclesiastical nature. It is a sad and sorry tiling— A source of lamentation— That Parish Councils. for the Xing. Should boss the blesse Nation. • It's killed the tine when voters all. Rejoiced to sit in fetters Owniqg the Squire trom the Nall. And the Parsou for their betters

This week the Medical Officer of Health for the Runcorn district has produced his annual report on the health of the district, from whicd it appears that the Runcorn Urban District Council is to be congratulated upon the sanitation of tqe district I All I can say is much good work has been done by ' the klealth Committee; but there is a great deal • more remaining to be done, and whilst crAliting them for accomplishments, the omission of many ' things must not be forgotten. Toe good health enjoyed by Runcorn is more markedly due, now. ever, to its natural situation and the blessings of the Creator, than to either its drainage, water, or other sanitary qualities.

The Runcorn Rural District Council and Board of Guardians will meet for their annual meeting on Tuesday week, and will have tn pick Chairmen for both bodies. As both Board and Council will be again almost similarly constituted, it might be that the gentlemen lately holding the positions will be 'called upon to continue in their Several capacities. All are men who in the past have conducted the business with despatch and dignity; and the only effect a change would have would be the handing onof the honour,for it would ba difficult to change for the better.

Mr S Woodward has promised to raise up a legacy of the " old " for the " new " body, in the shape of the Isolation Hospital question, upon which a peculiar discussion took place on Tuesday last. In fact, the discus Lion was a revelation and, it was only when Dr Adams had finished speaking, that the Council seemed to really become aware of "where they were"! The debate was certainly in- congruous, and one hardly to be expected from an up-to-date Council. Personally, I must admit that the history of the hospital question lay in obscurity, 'so far as I was concerned, or I would have com- mented long ego.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

For the match at Batley, on Saturday, in the 4th round of the Northern Union Cup, the Rancorn committee on Wednesday night selected the follow- ing team: Houghton, hack; D Jones, Richardson, Butterworth and Warder, three-guarte backs; Jolley and Faulkner, half backs; Walker, Farmer, Lightfoot, Reece, Tomlinson, J Langley, and Messenger, forwards. Although Warder is chosen, it is by no means certain that he will be able to play. He has been incapacitated since the Swinton match, but resumed work yesterday. It he fe-ls fit on Saturday he will turn out. In his absence Herbert Jones will officiate on the wing.

A measure of praise is due to several of the Run- corn plhyers for last Saturday's display, and were 1 to fail to single out Langley (the forward) for 'pedal mention, I would be falling short of my duty. Walker was good too, and Gayter and Light- foot were also steady and always on the move, I could telllhow Farmer got his try,but preferluot to. Suffice it, he was given a chance and took ir. Jolley I and Faulkner, tne halves, did wonders; but then such is always expected of them. The three-quarter line, perhaps, was about the rockiest that ever I figured for Runcorn in any match. Jimmy Butter- I worth was tt,ere, but not the "Jimmy "of old, and as for the other three, Rtchardson, D. Jones and 11. Jones, practically speaking, they are all youngsters, and hove their " spurs" to win; yet, it is true, War- der, Wilkinson, and the rest of the old hands were never missed. Houghton was "Houghton," and when that is said, we know how he flqured.

For the visitors, it must be grant?d that their forwards several times sh3wed spirit and gained possession many a time to the disadvantage of the home lot, but laths open they were a long way short. Perhaps York's best an was Grace (the half back). and their next best Jacqu >ll (at three- quarters) • but, as for the rest, there was "a much of • muchness "about them, and they are welcome to quarrel for next mention if they like, for the drubbing they got was fully indicative of their share of the game.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION CUP
div.p: NORTHERN UNION CUP
COMPETITION.
THIRD ROUND.
Warrington v. Leeds Parish Church.

The third round of the Northern Union Cup Compe- tition brought Warrington in contact with another Leeds Club—the Parish Church—who came to Wilderspool with a following ot about 700 spectaors,and fully determined to smite the "wire pullers" hip and thigh it poisible. They were fully represented, and the home team also turned out as selected. Splendid football weather favoured the fiatute and the ground was in perfect con- dition. A fine crowd assembled, the ground being wet- filled, especially on the popular side where the great ma- jority of the 7,000 spectators were congregated Mr. Oak land, of Outwood Church. was the referee and the teams lined out in the following order. Warrington :—Ballam, full-back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris, thret-quarters ; Bate and Duck- worth, half-backs ; Boardman, Fell, Edmondson, Eden, Scholtze, Swift, Mereweather, and Cunningham, for- wards. Leeds Parish Church :—Corcoran, full-back ; Smith, Het berts,Evans,and B-ivien, three-quarters ; Mosley and Knight, halfbacks; Birch, Crompton, Davison, Fester, M'N 'cholas, Taylor,Tlson,and Wainwright, forwards. M'Nicholas started with the wind, Barris responding by running into the Leeds half, but the visitora got the upper band, and as the result of powerful forward play, ,! Warrington bad to defend for some time. Mosley wee very active behind the scrimmage, and a short punt by him caused Hallam to be grassed on his line. Stern work followed, the borne defence being severely tested Bate pur.ted out, Corcoran missing a mark opposite the poste, from which Mosely was unable to niece a goal Another rush by the Leeds vanguard brake through the home defence, Hallam saving brilliantly near the poets. Leeds were bolding all the advan,age in the packs, but Duckworth and Bate finally enabled Warrington to take up the attack. A 'fine bout of passing was just ntaied in the bud on the line, where Dickenson was broach!' down by Corcoran. Fur:her passing gave Fish possession, and be dashed in at the corner, nely to lose the ball xi he was tackled. The Le-' s for. ' wards woke up again, and forced play t) the quarter-line. Here, Isherwood seappel up, and , a quick pass to Fish gave the latter an oppoitanity, which he fully utilised, by dodging through year the corner. The scorer took the goal kick, and had hard luck in seeing the ball bouace back off the or .84-bar. Parish Church forced Warrington beck, Knight and Mosley making's gallant effort, which just fell short of success as the whistle sounded for half-tima. Warring- ton were leading ty a try to nil when Swift re-started. Keen play followed, the Yorkshirernen five- threequarters, and still winning in rhq packs. Warring- ton could make no headway for Isoms time, but they succeeded in keeping the Parish backs well in hand. The tackling was exceptionally vigorous, and Mr Oakland had to caution a couple of burly Leeds forwards. At last, a magnificent piece of play by tha Warringten half backs resulted in a second try by Isherwood, but Fitt failed at goal. Toe Parish still struggled on, and Evans made a couple of powerful 111129 to the centre only to fall a Victim to Fah each time. Helium sent the Leeds _

men to the rightab nit once more, and Harris taking ; had pass from Bate. forced bis way over at the corner. Fish,who had just previously hit the post with a penalty kick, again trot( the place, and, on the call of time, landed a good goal. Final.—Warrington one goal and three tries (11 points), to Parish Church nil.
Runcorn v. York.

This match came off at the Imoll-lane enclosure, on Saturday list, nothwithstanding that the" York folk" had tried their level best, with a " gilded pill," to get the match played there. Some 200 Yirkists journeyed with their favourite, and when hostilities commenced there would. be abcut 3,000 spectators present. The composition of the teams was as follows . Runcorn.—Boughton, back ; D Jones, Butterworth, Rii•hardson, and H Jones, three-quarters ; Faulkner and Jolley, halves ; Walker, Reece, Farmer, Lightfoot, ' , Gayter, Woods, Messenger and Langley, forwards. Yorko—Lotthous,,. back; Goodyear, Bellerby,Jacques, Fletcher, three-quarters ; brace and Hayes, ba;vee, ; I Hope, Neale, Pick.ird, Ronson, Smith, Stead, Wade- worth, and Wooley, forwards. It fell to York to start the game, and they did so with a dash that brooked ill for Runcorn's chances, Immedi- ately, there were some grand exchanges, but the visitors appeared to be going with the greatest sting. Five minutes play, however, saw a waning of the visitors efforts, and a corresponding vigour seemed to animate the Runcorn men: Indeed, the change became so marked, that from that moment the issue of the game was never in doubt. Faulkner first set hia hacks on the attack.and a moment later Jolley was ea evidence. Oran- and Jacques, however, replied very effectively, but only gained temporary relief. Runcorn pressed with re- markable tact, only Co fall back ,before a capable move- ment on the part of Rlllerby and Goodyear. Houghton, who was playing up right behind his men did not, however, let the ball get any further than the half-way. Jolley added to the excitement with judicious kicking and Langley and Walker were also conspicuous for the exceptional way they followed up. York forwards then got dangerously near Hough- ton's charge, and Jacques dropped for goal, just being a trifle short, Woods ot Runcorn, and Wadaworth, of York, then interchanged sundry kicks, but as th,y were not kicking the ball, the linesman drew the referee's attention to the mater, and both were ordered off. On resuming, Houghton put in a characteristic run. Off- side ,'ay by a York forward then enabled the home men to attack the visitors' line repeatedly. Loftrearse was sorely taxed, and the home aide threw at least one chance clean away. Amends were made a little later; Faulk or fairly bluffing bis opponents ; by pretending to go for the line himself, he drew most of the defenders to big own side of the field, then, with a long pas% sent to Richardson who enabled H • Jones to score at the corner. Jolley converted. Continuing to keep York on the de- fence, Runcorn made several attempts to increae their lead. Butterworth had the first opening, but failed ye take Jolley's pass. D. Jones did likewise, and a penalty kink eenbled York to clear. Later, Jolley took a penalty and landed a goal. Fine kicking, good tackling, and fair passing were now indulged in by both teams, but the visitors seemed lost at the bewildering way in which the home forwards played, for they were here, there and everywhere. A rather lucky try then fell to the home team, The ball, coming out of a melee, was kicked by Messenger to U Jon?s, and he picking up scot, d rai her unexpectedly. Jolley had a good shot at goal but failed. Butterworth dropped a further goat. Rnncorn right to the intervsl kept the master hand,and the teams crossed over with the Spore Runcorn three goal, two tries: York nil.

The second half opened in tbe same brisk war 'DS the first, but this time it was the home men that made the pace. It was quite clear that the Yorkists had met a superior combination, and that they were going to be heaten. tiU, the visitors never once gave up,and were ropcnaible for many good an 1 capable dashes for the bony, line. Houghton saved always in his best style, and Tolley as an earns back in times of danger was always doing the right thing. Play for s long time re- mained in the visitors' quarters,and before the seige was lifted Hichardaon had scored a couple of tries, as finish• ing touches to good play on the part of his colleagues. Grace, Jacques, and Fletcher were then resnoneible for a big effort. This was baulked by a smart counter more of Fau!kner's. Grace then got the who!e of the York men on the," pass," but instead or gaining they lost ground, with the reFult that Jolley had a dash for their line only to be hd up. Houghton then tii.A to score, ad in tckling him Neale got bort and had to retire. With this added disadvantage York found themselves unable to stem the tide of adversity, and as the result ,of a forward rush Farmer succeeded in scoring. Jolley missed the goal. Subsequent to this it was noticed the home team scarcely exerted themselves, and at the close of the game York were making strenuous but unavail- ing efforts to pierce the home defence. Final : liuncern 3 goals, 5 tries, 21 points ; York, nil.

div.head: Birkenhead Wanderers v. Widnes.
div.p: Birkenhead Wanderers v. Widnes.

At Birkenhead, before about 2,000 spectators, Widnes won the toss, and Harris started for the Wanderere,whe were immediately penalised, Batey' s kick going dead. Play was very fast, bosh teams pressing in turn. From a mark Batey almost landed a •sioal for Widues, after which the game was delayed through an injury to Aspey. Eventually Widees attacked in earnest feshion, and Peacock ran over the corner, Situ missing at the place. Widnes still continued to press, and Peacock a,ain , scored, Batey landing a goal. The Wanderers tried hard to make headway, but were very spasmodic and seldom did the right thing. Harris tried at gat from a mark, but kicked short: Nothing farther was done in the first half, which saw Widnes leading by eight points to nil. On restarting play was very keenly cautested. The Wanderers showed improved form, but Widnes had ,-as- tablished too big a lead, and they failed to get on terms. Batey and Harris respectively kicked goals. Result : Widnes, 10 plaints ; Birkenhead Wanderers, two points. St. Helens v. Batley. At St Helens before about 7,000 spectators. Batley played downhill at the outset, and had much the best of the play, pressing hard. Davies ultimately gained pos- session in the centre, and eluding his opponents, ran in a try near the corner, the same player just failing to add a goal. Doherty and Foulkes exhibited capital de- fensive play, but the visitors were in splendid form, and from a mark by Rogers, Davies kclited a goal, giving Batley a lead of five points. From a pass by Morris, Hunter gained a try between the uprights, and Traynor added a goal. Half-time :.--St Helens, one goal and one try; Batley, one goal and one try. On ends being changed the Batley men had rather the beet of the play, From • scrimmage near the home 25 line Fitzgerald gained possession and again gave Batley the lead by dropping a goal. The St Helens men then dribbled down in a body, and Fossall saved near his line. S. Heli as played hard to score, and Fitzgerald stopped a rush by Liversage and Hunter. From a mark, Trayor dropped the ball in front of the Batley posts, which ended in Oakland cleverly touching down. Traynor stopped a dribbl3 by several Batley forwards. St Helens gradually forced them back, and scrummaging play in the Batley quarters followel. Traynor failed to place a goal from an easy, position facing goal. There was no further scoring Riem.t :—Batley,, two goals and one try (seven points) ; St Helens. one goal and one try (five points). Broughton Rangers v. Oldham. This mach was played on the Ringers ground, in splendid weather, before upwards of 18,000 spectators. Bath clubs were strongly represented After wo T11,1510t5 had fallen to Oldham, ,he Rangers took up the attack, and from a mark by Winskill, W James kicked a goal. Shortly afterwards Thomas deliberately knocked the ball away from one of the home forwards, and Oldham were penalised, but W James failed to place a goal from an easy polition. Then the Oldham three-quarters got off with a fine combined movement, which ended in Davies scoring :en unimproved try, and ends were changed with °Ahem .leading by three points to two Previous to Davies icon' g. Chapman was badly hurt, and had to be carried off the ground, and throughout the second half the Rangers placed a man short. Quickly Oldham showed superior passing and A. Lees dodged own from a eerummege, but no goal resulted. This made the score six points to two, bat when W James dropped a splendid goat from over the half way line the excitement was great. The Rangers attacked, and for a short time penned Oldham on their line. Further misfortune, however, befel the Rangers as the ball was kicked to Harry, who tan toaneet it, but it bounced away from him, and Huzzey,following well got possession and passed to A. Lies, who had no d'ffi- culty in scoring a try behind the pests. flozzey placed a goal. Thie decided the game, and Cedhana won by eleven points to four. Score :—Oldham, one goal and three tries (11 points) ; Broueleton Rangers, two goals (four points).
Brighouse Rangers v. Hull Kingston Rovers-

At Lane Head, Brighouse, before 6,000 apectstore Nicholl kicked off for Brighouse. After a spell of pres- sure Tullock dropped at goal, but the ball glanced out- side the upright. From the drop-out play ruled even for ROllle time, but eventually Brighouse were hard pressel, and from a kick by Denham Moffitt made a free ' cstch f. or Kemp to kick a goal. shortly after Brigooule Iwere penalised, but Kemp failed at goal. Saville almost placed a goal, the ball rebounding from the crossbar. Brighouse again pressed. At half-time Hull led by a goal to nil. Almost immediately after the recommence- ment Phipps made his mark in a good position. The succeeding play WAR fairly even. until Morfitt grit hold near his own line. He set elf up the field, kicking when Barker pressed him hard. Tullock tsrkled Saville with the ball on his own line,and altegether Hull assemed the upper hand, confining Brighouse to their own qusr- tees, despite the fact that Hull were eperating up the slope, Robinson got off, kicked, again secured, Pass" to Morfitt,who scored behind the poets.but Kemp failed at goal. Result :—Efull, two goals and one try (seven points) ; Brighouse, nil. Wakefield v. Bradford. Fully 20,000 spectators witnessed this match. Wake- field started, and after 14 minutes' 'slay Metcalfe, from Whitaker's mark, placed a goal, subsequently adding a eecond goal from a penalty kick. Half-time : Wakefield, two goals (four points) ; Bradford, nil. Watson kicked off, and the play was at once taken to the Bradford half, Bennett mulled,and consequently Brselford got a footing in the home half. By short stages the visitors' goal was reached, but Heseltine and Feather relieved with a neat passing run to the Wakefield quarter line, and Cooper almost got in. Goodyear relieving with a good kick rh. Bradford quarter line being reached, a scrummage ensued on the line, nothing being ssored, Metcalfe kick- ing the tall over the line goon after. Wakefield still pressed. Heseltine kicked down to Metcilfe,otho put in a weak kick, and Feather got close to the home Inc. Cooper mimed in • favourable position, hut failed to raise the ball. Bradford tried hard to score, Wakefield being hardly preieed, Evers eventually getting over under the posts. Cooper kicked a goal, giving Bradford ' a point lead. The play after the kick-out turd in favour of Wakefield, being inside the Bradford half most of the ' time, Balmforth, Goodyear, and 3ennett taking the 1 play close to the line, Ward and Pollard relieving Mars- den dropped at goal, a minor only accruing. Result : Bradford. one goal and ono, try (five points) ; Wakefield, two goals (four paints). Dewsbury V. Castleford. Before 5,000 spectators, at Dewsbury. Halftime : ICastleford, one goal pswsburv, nil. hum diately after Ithe change of ends Burns crossed the Dewsbury line, Smith failing at goal. Pearson, after junsrt passing by Lockwood. scored a try fee Dewsbury. R-eult :—Castle- ford, one goal and one try (five points) ; Dewsbury, one try (three points).

div.head: HIS CAP STUCK TO HIS HEAD,
div.p: HIS CAP STUCK TO HIS HEAD,
If this story were spun out to its full length it would fill a column of fits print ; for it is virtually a man's biography. But life is short and tales should be the same.

" As boys," the man says, " we used to play around an old treo near my home. One day when I was about fourteen a bey companion and I were romping there. Oa trying for some reason to remove my cAp I found I couldn't do it ; the cap positively stuck to my bead as if it were glued on.

" Frightened at this, I ran into the house to my mother. With bomu trouble, and no little fuss and whimpering on my part, she pulled the cap off and saw. to Oar am.zement, that the top of my head was white as though it had just been dipped in milk.

"This was to me the beginning of many wretched years. Scales lormed over my eyes, almost blinding me. I was treated at the Old Sr. Thomas' Hospital and after- wards at Guy's, but got no lattter. Medicines and °int- ' ments wore wasted on me. My parents took me to the ' seaside and let me wallow in the mud. Many a time did my father take me to Brighton, whir° he buried me to the neck in the mud, and rubbed the nasty stuff into every part of my body. The mud washed off, but the disease remained. Oacs I tried a famous 'herbal' ointment at is. 11 d per box. I ended witb a big pile of empty boxes and the skin eruption. Only toe ointment and my money were gone. From time to tine I attendad various skin hospitals. The doctors looked solemn and talked learned- ly, but when I left I took my tormenting malady with mo, no science was able to rid me of that. I especially dreaded the Spring and fall As I was always much worse then. What I suffered in body and mind is more than I can put in words.

" In the early part of 1899 1 read of the power of Mother Seiizei'm Syrup as a blood purifliAr and began using it. In less than a month the scabs and sores on my che back and legs began to disappear; and before I nad finished the third 2s ed bottle they were gone, together with a troublesome spot in the bend of the knee, which had never once left me for forty years:

"To day my ikin is 'so-ft and white as a healthy child It aiiybAy doubts this let him write, or visit me. All I wish to add is that Mo her Seigel's Syrup is the most wonderful cleanser of the blood seen on earth since Naaman was miraculously healed in the river Jordan."—George Robeit Kirby, 173, Blackhorse-road, St Andrew's-road, Waltharnit9w, Ewa, January 9th, 1900. Declared January 15t , 1900, at Walthamstow, before William Dunlop Cunniniiham, Commissioner for Oaths in the Supreme Court of Judicature.
Mr. Kirby is now in the employ of the Urban District Council of Waltbamstow.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSUCIATI ON.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSUCIATI ON.
Address by Miss Shilston.

A drawing-e:ren meeting in connection with tee above-named A sociation was held (by permission of the Mayor) in the Town Hall, Warrington, on Friday after- noon. There was a very encouraging attendance, the retesting bring presided over by the Mayorees (Mrs. Henry Roberts.) The president of the Association (Miss Be,sie Ductoe) explained that Mrs. 1. E Powell and Mrs. E R. 'rerbuck were unable to be present. The MAYORESS made a few introductory remarks in which she ez en led a hearty welcome co all present. She expri sied her pleasure at seeing such a large gather- hog, and in rale: ring to the influence which women were ' able to ex .Ft in the cause of temperance, she pleaded thst although inane of them were indisposed to speak in public oei the subject they could exert an individual I. fleence in their o orn social sphere which would have ceeisiderable f ffect. Miss SLIILSTON then dehverad an interesting address, je referring to the new century she •aid they ought to I feel very grateful that their lives land been cast in days when they, as women, were able to exert an kflueoce in the world which as denied to the women of the same c ass and Berne nationality, a hundred years ago. Tee difference was sery marked, owing to various forces which had changed the whole face of society dur- ing the 19th century. The • two chit forces which bad brought about this change were probably ehication and the application of steam and machinery to the varieus arts of life, Mess Shilston Pointed out that much of the work which was formerly done by woinen at home was now done in large factories and the work is the home had been con- siderably reduced. Probably of more importance w*s the marvellous advancement in the education of women. When it was proposed to educate women and young girls, bands were held up in righteous iedignetion. It was contended by many that education would totally unfit women for their sphere in life, it would unsex them if they were educal eJ. Women's place,it was said,was th 3 home and she shonld confine her es 'aviation to the ordinary domestic arts. The gift of education had quickened their sym- pathies and activities and bad widened their sphere of influence. At the present time, at the beginning of the 'new century,they as women •nd members of a women's organisation were just at a testing tim The time had gone by when the novelty of a women's organisation drew crowds and attracted notice. They should lay upon their hearts and consciences the abaolute necetesity ot showing and proving to the outside world, that the Association was of value and that It did count for good and that it wonted for the uplift of the society in which they were placed. It was necessary for them to throw off all apathy and enter upon their work with enthusiasm. rho speaker proceeded tea show how the association could be made a force as a temperance oreanizition by educating the pablic opinion on temper- ance matters. Speaking ot alcohol, she referred to it as a pnieon and explained its injurious effects upon the body. In addition to their individual responsibility and educational work, the members of that Association had got to realize that there was a great deal of social work to be due, It was said that women were nonentities in the political world, but as an illustratien t the con- trary, she might mention the splendid work which had been done by Miss Harriet Johidon in connection with the Sale of Drink to Children Bill. It was chie to her work in Liverpool that the justices or that city were led to draw up a resolution with reference to the sale of drink to children and this had led to to the agitation for a Bill to make it a pee-s 1 offence. Miss Johnsen had dote) a tremendous amount of organic akin work and they had now strong evider ce of general public sempathy in support of the Bill. One woman had done that by means of organie bon and there was no one, however small her iefluence might be, whe was unable to do anything. In conclu- sion she appealed to those present to use their influence on Sc half of temperance. • Mies Durres also spleke. In alluding to the passing of the second reading of the sale of Intoxicant. to Coil- dren's Bill, she said she was glad it had passed by such a large mai irity. She regretted that the member for Warrington had net voted in favour of the Bill. She noticed that the name of Mr Pierpoiut appeared amongst thope who voted against It. She regretted to see it, for she would have liked him to have been in sympathy with the movemtnt.

Town Hell, Mrs. Join,' FAIRCLOUGH sPconded the vote of thanks, which was crodially carried. The MAYOUESS and Miss SIIILSTON having ackco the compliment, afternoon tea wee pdrtaken of.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. A meeting of this Board was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse oe Wednesday moraine. Mr A J Jolley presided, and there were also present :—Hev J Riddette, Rev T R Matthews, Mrs Clay,Messra S Davies, J Clarke, William Houghton, A Brooks, J Maine, T LI Ashcroft, William Hickman, T B Malkin, R Forshaw, G Pilling, A Jolley, with J C Sutton (clerk), S Suttees (assistant clerk.), C H Ward (master), I Wright (super- intendent Padgate Schools). HOUSE COMMITTEE. At a meeting held on Friday, March 1511, the tenders for stone, drapery, groceries, and provisions and .cord and twill having been opened, it was resolved after con- sideration to accept for stone, Warrington Slate Com- pany, Limited ; draperies, etc Mr T J Lee ; groceries, and provisions, Messrs Richardson and Son ; cord and twill, Mr T J Lee. The master was empowered to inspect the firewood offered by Mr 11 Ileatnn, and if suitable, to purchase some at the rate of 163 6d per ton, delivered at the Workhouse. It was resolved that Miss Edith Mary Ward be appointed assistant matron at the rate ot salary of £3O per annum with rations dm, duties to commence at once. At a further meeting on March 221 d, Messrs Richard- son and Son having written respecting tender for groceries and provisions saying their tender was subject' to any additions that might lea put on by the Govern- ment in their next budget, the letter was considered and the terms accepted. The offer of Robert Heaton to supply 100 tons of firewood sleepers at 16, 6A delivered was accepted, the master having made a favourable report. Mr iliciemAN moved the confirmation of the minutes. Mr BROOKS stemided. The Rev J H timpErrir referred to the minute relating to the appointment of Miss Ward as assistant matron, and asked whether they were to understane that Miss Ward's position carried with it the privileges of a pen- sion. The CHAIRMAN : Certainly. She comes under the benefit of the Superannuation Act. • The Rev. J H RIDDETTE asked whether Miss Ward was being appointed to succeed a person whe was simply assistant to the matron. That was a dietinctioa whinh he found some members did not quite realise. He did not raise the question in any conteatious spirit. He had not the slightest objection to the appointment of Miss _Ward, but if they were appointing an assistant matron and thereby creating a permanent office involving cere Cain privileges, be would like to ask whether the prin- ciple bad been discussed by the Board? The CHAIRMAN The Board delegated certain powera to the House Committee with reference to it. The Rev J U RIDDETTE thought it was desirable that the matter should be reconsidered. All the members of the Board understood that under the pressure of duties on the matron, who had served them so well for many years, it became necessary to give her an assistant. The question arose whether the assistant was to be called an assistant to the matron or assistant matron—a distinc- tion with an important difference, let cause the office of assistant matron would be a permanent office and the two offices of matron and assistant matron would exist until the Board by resolution abolished one office. By appointing MiBS Ward to the office of assistant matron the Board was creating a now office and became liable for pension allowances. The CHAIRMAN said a little misapprehens'on seemed to exist with reference to the appointment. It could be terminated at a month's notice. As regard pensions, the new act applied to all the efficers of the Union. Ttie Rev J H Rinmerre : That i 3 because the act has come into operation since we appointed an assistant ta the matron. The CHAIRMAN : Yes; I think the ac a was passed in 1898. Mr Ataciaore said the Board was told a fortnight since that this appointment was only going to be a temporary one. , The CHAiRmAte : That is not correct. The CLBRK : Any invalidity of that kind is covered by the notice I have sent to every Guardian. The Rev J H RH:lowers then asked wbether thtre was a substautial difference between the tender of Messrs Richard Evans and Company, Limited, and tbat of the firm which had received the contract. Mr Emmert replied that the acceptance of the new contract would make a difference of £lOO during the half-year: Referro g to the appointment of Miss Ward as assistant matron, he said the committee was unanimous in recommending the appointmenc. There was a discussion as to whether she should be appointed assietant matron or an assistant to the matron and an amendment was moved but the resolution was carried in its present form. He supposed it would be a permanent appointment and he had no doubt Miss Ward would become a capable officer and of great service to the Union. They had found by experience that assist- ants to the matron did not atop very long, and that was a strong argument for making the appointment a per- manent one. The Rev J H RIDDETTE said he had been told that Miss Ward received a salary for the work aloe did as music teacher. The CHAIRMAN: Certainly not. The Rev T R MATTHEWS said he was perhaps Teener'- , sible for the queetion. In reply to a question asked some years ago be was told that Miss Ward was a paid officer of the Union in consequence of her position as organist. The CHAIRMAN pointed out that Miss Ward did at one time receive a small honorarium for her services in the capacity indicated but in recent years she had performed the office voluntarily without any pay whatever. The minutes were then passed. GIFTS. The Workhouse Master acknowledged gifts as follows —papers from the chaplain, Rev E R Tarbuck, Mr T H Ate-croft, and Miss Watkin, matron of the Infirmary. Mr Owen presented a large picture to be hung in the matron's room and one for the medical officer's room, for which he was heartily thanked.' It was also reported that 6 boys and 10 girls were con- firmed in Hollinfare Chutch on March 23rd. CLERK'S SrATEMENP UPON THE ESTIMATES. Tin CREEK presented his statement upon the estimates for the hall-year ending at Michaelmas, 1901, which showed that the common charges and contributions reqnired from the Union townships ameunted to a tote; of £13,038 Si as compared with £ll 872 be 91 in th preceding 3 ear. Estimated receipls at £3,099 brought down the present estimate to £9,939 Si. The substantial increase provided for in maintenance tee Clerk says, is to cover increases of cost of provisions and nee< ssariee, and any addition that may result from amended dietary tables. A necessarily increased workhouse and infirmary; staff cccasions a promo tional addition to salary and ration ace nrnts. Improved annual value of uninn assessable property is attended by heavier claims for rates. The charge for maintenance of lunatics' at the several county asylums is raised by sevenpence per head per week, hence a materiall addition to the preceding estimate. Under some other beads at outlay, as of registration and vaccination, growth of cost follows in ratio with growth of popula- tion. It is to be remembered that, although prudent to make so considerable an increased provision, it will not, follow that actual expenditure in the half-year will rise in equal proportion. It is satisfactory to advise that although about £5,000 has been, during the progrcia of the Infirmary. Electric and other works, expended with- out the aid of loan, the Union thereby being relieved alike of instalments of principal and charges for interest thereon, and althou4h, beyond the preparation muscle for the purposes set forth in these estimate, a further tem, exceeding £l,OOO, is to be applied to important Workhouse improvements, and although it is for the present anticipated that a further sum of over £2,000 for land and buildings at Etrlestown may be used,with- out resort to borrowing powers, the low sixpenny call of recent half-years may be again fixed upon, also to remember that this sixpence in the £ is the full true " Poor Rate." Cen'inuinge the Clerk says, papers explanatory of Union Estimates were first prepared in rnyllfirst year of effice as Chairman of the Board, and have been can- thmed during the period of my long service as Clerk. Examination of growth of local indebtedness, not of a !Reality, but of all the Kingdom, has been a frequent theme, treated of in a mild spirit of criticism. In this form has avoidance of avoidable loan debts been persiz- tently advocated, and a few lines now upon the result may be usefully introeuced in the present paper. Pur- chase of the Pedgate Estate and erection thereon of the noble Institution forming homes and schools for poor children had been impramicable without the aid of bor- rowing powers. Yet the procedure Guardians bad been long bent on was reluctantly delayed for rateable ' values to astume higher pr i portions, and for ease being. given to loan burdens. In like manner, year by year, for many a year in SucleSsion, was the more and more pressing need for improved and extended accommoda- tion for sick and helpless poor abided with, that assessable values might strengthen and Union loan deb's weaken, The purpose of; poesessing an Infirmary in no respect second to the best of institu- tions of the kind to be found elsewhere,without addition to local rates, has been achieved. Whereas the additiontl land, with buildings, fittings, and works have required '

an outlay of £40,020-the-Prisent total outstanding loan liabilities of toe Guardians, upAl all Union lands, build- ings and property, totals, £37,273, a debt that would be fully covered by a single rate.of 4103 iu the £ on the present Union Rateable value.' '

- A summary has usually been given; in papers of corresponding date with this, of important items of out- lay extracted from the annual poor rate retusn,prepared in my department for the Local Government Beard, of reoeipts by overseers in each year ending at Lady Day. Without detailing so fully es u mil particulars thereof,it I may be recorded that in the yea ending at Lady Day, 11900, the overseers of your parishes collected as ' poor rates" £48,092, receiving from other sources £276,t0tal £48,368. Your board received of that Rim £27,507, and paid thereout to the administrative County £8,605 as county rates. The CHArrimAN thought the Board would be satisfied that the charge for common fund purposes did not exceed sixpence in the Z. (Hear,-bear,) £lOO FOR THE CLERK. Mr WILLIAM HOIIGRTOX moved the following resolu- tion of the Infirmary Committee :—" That pursuant to the standing order in that behalf, and subject to appro- val by the Local Government Board, the Clerk Le paid a sum of £lOO for services rendered by him, and in his department, outside his ordinary duties as Clerk of the Board, such extra services having been rendered in the years 1896 to 1901. The grant to include hie services in respect of land purchase, loans, contracts, infirmary and other works, also to include 'services in connection with Earlestown land and buildings and Workhouse altera- tions." .„ Mr William HicxstaN seconded the resolution, and said the Clerk well deserved the suna proposed to be given for the extra work he had done in connectien with the building of the new infirmary, the purchase of land,. and offices, Ice., and the money he had saved the Board and the ratepayers. Mr AsiicaCYT said he had great pleasure in supporting the resolution. It was unanimously carried. THE WORKHOUSE AL FERATIONS. The CLERK reported that he had received an order from the Local Government Board sanctioning the ex- penditure of £1,003 upon workhouse alterations. EXAMINATION OF WORKHOUSE CHILDREN. The CLERK reported that be nad received a letter from Mr at zley , inspector of Union Schoch, stating that he would attend on Wednesday and Thursday, April 3rd and 4th, for the purpose of examining the children. Be would commence the exarniustion of the girls at 10.20 o'clock on Wednesday and the boys at 9 o'clock on Thursday. , INCREASE IN THE COS t' OF LUNATICS. The Lancashire Asylums Board forwarded a statement that the cost of maintenance per head per week of the inmates In the several asylums in the county was to be raised from 83 91 to 93 4d. The CLERK added that the iucroaso was probably due to the increased cost of coal. 2 war guardians SUPERANNUATION ALLOWANCE DEDUCTION. The CLERK said be had received a letter from Mr Jack son, father of one of the officers of the Union, complain- ing of the deduction made for superannuation allowance The Clerk pointed out that under the new superanuation act, all officers, except nurses, must pay towards the uperanuation allowance MR. SHEARER'S SALARY, The Local Governmeut Board wrote approving of the increase of £25 to Mr Shearer's salary. ASSESSMENTS. A communication was reed seating that the County Rate Joint Committee were anxious to go rouud for the purpose of ascertaining the system adopted in the dif- ferent unions for fixing assessments. The Committee would visit Warrington on the 12th April and the Union Assessment Committee was requested to meet them. This was all the business.

div.head: SERIOUS FIRE AT PENKETH.
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE AT PENKETH.
Messrs. Garnett's Works Gutted. Heavy Damage.

Early on Wednesday morning the Penketh works of Messrs R Garnett & Sons, the well-known firm of cabinet makers, were the scene of a disastrous fire. The outbreak was discovered shortly before live o'clock, and the fire brigade of the Penketh Tanning Company immediately turned out. The pressure from the water mains was however very poor. In the meantime Mr Owen, junior had cycled to Warrington and given the alarm to the Warrington Fire Brigade. Superintendent Turner and a full complement of men turned out with remarkable promptitude with the steam engine" Major." By the time they arrived at the scene of the conflsgration the flumes had spread with great rapidity, shooting up to a height ofJ twenty or thirty feet. The Penketh Brigade had confined their efforts to the eaving of two adjoining cottages, and the furniture had been hurriedly removed into the road. Their efforts in this direc- tion were rewarded with success: The Warrington Brigade lost no time in getting to work, and soon had three powerful jets playing. It soon became evident that the workshops were doomed, and to prevent any accident the Superin- tendent deemed it wise to have the front wall adjoinieg Widnes-read pulled down. While this was being done the captain of the Penketh Brigade was struck in the stomach by a piece of falling timber. The injury was not, however, serious, and be was able to walk home. The firemen afterward directed their efforts to saving one of the store- rooms and several valuable stacks of timber, and, working energetically, were highly suc,cesstul, and saved nearly the whole of the stock of timber and the storeroom. 'I he remainder of the premises was gutted, and only a mass of debris was to be seen later in the morning. The firemen, however, continued to pour volumes of water on the smoking ruins. Several minor outbreaks occurred, but these were speedily extinguished. The great heat which the fire caused may belimagined from the fact that the doors and other wodwork of the cottages adjoin- ing were severely scorched. Fortunately there was little or no wind from the west, otherwise the whole of the property must in- evitably hate been destroyed. As it was thefdamage was very great. Not one wall in the inside of the building was standing. The timber which was saved consisted of some well seasoned mahogany, and a quantity of other valuable woods. It is in- tereeting to note that this mahogany also escaped the ravages of the flames at the great fire at the Canada Dock, where it was stocked some years ago. The whole of the machinery and workmen's tools were destroyed. The building is an old one,baving tabletebearing the dates 1849, 1857, and 1894,the latter dates being those of enlargements. The outbreak originated near the boilers, and at midnight, when Police-con- stable Houghton, passed the works, there was nothing to arouse his suspicions. Mr Garnett was on the premises at five o'clock on Tuesday evening, and the men left at 6 30, when everything was apparently safts. The fire caused great excitement in the village,and almost the whole of the population turned out to witness it. Some very important contracts were in hand from banks, private offices, and private individuals, but, fortunately, Messrs Garnett have additional workshops with ever' necessary facility for re- executing all work in hand with the least possible delay. PlThe Warrington Fire Brigade returned to town at 12 40, having been away over seven hours.

The police were notified on the 24th inst of the sudden death of Sarah Dutton, 81 yPara old, widow of the late George Dutton, shoemaker, The old lady had lived at 143. Legh-ptreet, the residence of her son, John Dutton. and her death occurred about 10 o'clnck on the night of the 23rd inst. For about three years prior to her death phe had lived at 59, Regent-street, F arlestown, and on the 7th inst she fell from a chair on the floor and fractured her left thigh. div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON,
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON,

ESA. The usual weekly meeting of the Earlestown and District P.S.A.. Society.was held in the Co-operative Hall on Sunday afteroon, there bein4 again a fair attendance of members. Mr J Jackson presided, and he delivered an interesting address. Local items were submitted by Miss L Jones, and Miss Harvey officiated at the piano. EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON PHOTOGRAPHIC SOCIETY.

In tonnection with the society a musical evening and lantern exhibition took place in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday night. The attendance was a very fair one and the pictures thrown on the ecreen,included abont 209 slides pre- pared solely by members of the Society, embracing types of mankind, scenes from the Transvaal War, local scenery portraits, humorous subjects,&c. The musical programme was sustained by Miss Edith Sirett " Ever of thee " and " Tatters " ; Mr Mather "The death of Nelson "and "Mary of Argyle" ; Mr S Dring "The Village Blacksmith," and "'Neath the rolling tide." The various songs were illustrated by the lantern. PIONEER LECTURES AT Eatimcsrowx. The laA lecture of the series promoted by the Newton-in-Makerfield Lectures Cimmittee was &livered in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Wed- nesday evening before a large audience, The subject was" Explosives and Explosion'," and it should really have been tbe first lecture of the course, but owing to unavoidable circumstances it bad to be Postponed until the present data. Mr Vyvian Lewis was the advertised lecturer, but owing to an acci- dent, he was unable to be present, his place being ably filled by Mr J S S Braname of Greenwich College. Lord Newton was announced to preside, but his parliamentary duties prevented his attend- ance, and Dr Handyside filled the vacancy. The lecturer proceeded with his explanation of the various kinds of exolosiveri,detailing at length their composition and effect, and his discourse was rend- ered more interesting by elaborate experiment". A vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer and chairman at the close. A FATAL FALL DOWNSTATRS. On Wednesday morning an inquest was held at the Town Hall, Earlestown, by Mr S Brighouse, coroner, on the body of Thomas Glynn, 53 years old, a labourer in the Sanitary Depot of the Newton Urban District Council, who died from injuries received by falling down the stairs leading from the club room of the Irish National League in Back Market-street, Earlestown, on the 22nd inst.— Thomas Glynn, son of the deceased, deposed that his father died at three o'clock on Tuesday. Witness said he saw his father at 8.30 p.m. on the 22nd boat at the Irish League club room. He was cheerful and in good health. tie bad had some drink, but was not drunk. De- ceased left the room and said good night to witness and several others. Shortly afterwards witness heard a crash, and on going to the head of the stairs saw his father lying at the bottom- He was , bleeding from a wound in the forehead. He was assisted up and walked home, and afterwards went to bed. Witness saw him next day and be com- plained of pains in the head. Witness had no reason to suspect foul play.—Dr Gauge, who at- tended deceased gave it as his opinion that death was due to cerebral hmmorrhage.—A verdict of accidental death was given, the jury suggesting that a hand rail should be fixed to the wall of the stairs.

div.head: DARING BURGLARIES AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: DARING BURGLARIES AT EARLES- TOWN.
Two Shops Entered.

During Friday night, Earlesto ma was visited by a gang of burglars, who centred their operations on the lock-up shoo of Messrs Howe and Son, toamen„ and the premises of Mr W Jonas, pawnbroker, situated in Mareet-street. An entrance was effected at the back of Mr Howe's shop, from which the other place was entered. About six o'clock on Saturday morning, Mr Morris, who is the manager for her Jones, was awakened by his dog, and on going downstairs found several men in the shop. Hearing Mr Morris, the men escaped by the back and scaled the will, one re-entering the tea shop and the other escaped over the roof. Search was made for the man and he was discovered on the roof of the room upstairs, covered up. He was taken to the police station. where he gave his name as James Anderson, of Man- :heater. It appears that the burglars sealed the wall at the back of Mr Howe's shop, and,breaking a window, undid the catch, but on getting inside found that the door leading to the shop was firmly locked en the inside. Nothing daunted, the thieves removed about a dozen bricks from the wall and made a bole large enough to crawl through. Not content with this damage, they took the lock bodily off the door. The thieves then tried the safe, which contained about £lOO, but fortunately it would not yield. Having thus been foiled, the gang returned to the back and removed a couple of iron bars from the window leading into Mr Jones's shop, and thus got into the shop. Two of the men ransacked the place, and after securing about 181 ira cash and several silk handkerchiefs prepared to:de- camp. At this time Mr Morris, the manager for Mr Jones, who lived on the premiles, having been roused by his dog, came down into the shop and immediately chased the burglars. The chase continued through the warehouse and window by which the entrance had been effected and over the wall. One man got away, but prisoner returned to Mr Howe's shop and Mr Morris gave the alarm, and Constable Brown and Peter Morrison, of Glebe-terrace, Haydock, John Huffier of Newton-terrace and William Isherwood of Isawrence-etreet were quickly on the scene. A search was made for the prisoner, who was eventually discovered secreted between the slates and the roof, with his cost thrown over his head. Mr Morris is to be highly complimented upon the plucky way in which he tackled the men, considering that they had brought a large bacon knife, a cleaver, and a steel from the tea shop to use in gaining entrance. The weapons were afterwarde discovered in the shop by Mr Morris. It is believed that the gang visited the Haydock Park races on Friday. Prisoner before the Magistrates. At the Esrlesrown Police Office, on Saturday, James Anderson, of Manchester, the man who was caught in connection with the burglary, was brought before Mr Emmett.—lnspector Morgan stated that Prisoner was charged with breaking and entering the look-up shop 540, Market-street, and also the premises 542. Market- street, some time during the night, and he (Inspector Morgan) would offer sufficient evidence to justify a re- mand until Monday.—Mr Henry Morris then gave evi- dence of his adventure that morning, and Mr Emmett remanded Anderson to Warrington.

At the quarterly meeting of the Couneil of the Royal Lancashire Agricultural Society held at Liver- pool on Wednesday, Mr John White, J P, of Moore Hall, who has been associated with the work of the society for 50 years, was elected vice-chairman of the Council.

Interesting Presentation at Warrington. An interesting presentation, took place in the Engineers' Office, of the Postal Telegraph Depart- ment, et Warrington, on Saturday, when Mr W Stevenson, engineer, was the recipient of a hand- some briei bag and fountain pen, Mr J Brown pre- sided, and was supported by Messrs. G Young, W Branwood, J Green, W Bennett, J Naylor, J Heath,' J P Charles, T Harrison, H Swindells. It Bradshaw and P Overend. Many other officials in the En- gineering Department were unavoidably absent. The Chairman said he felt sure he as expressing the sentiments of all when he stated they were sorry that Mr Stevenson was leaving the district Though his stay amongst them had been a short one he hoped be would go away with pleasant re- collections of hi s connection with them. He trusted that be would be happy in his new sphere, and,that success would crown his efforts. The Chairman then requested Mr George Young of Northwich, as senior officer in the district, to make the presenta- tion. Mr Young in doing ro said he could thoroughly endorse the remarks of the chairman. Mr Stevenson's stay in the district had been very brief; he had, however, .during his tenure of office, earned the kindly feelings and respect of the various staffs in the engineering department. This was obvious when he stated that,without exception every member of the staff had unhesitatiirgly con- tributed to the very handsome present which he was about to band over. This fact alone would be very gratifying to the recipient. Mr Stevenson's ser- vices had been very highly appreciated, and, on behalf of all concerned he wished him every success and trusted that he would live long to enjoy the honours conferred upon him. Mr Stevenson briefly returned thanks and said be had always en- deavoured to carry out his duties in a proper manner, and he was gratified to find that he had succeeded. He was deeply obliged for the kindly expressions, which he heartily reciprocated. Ap- propriate remarks were also made by Messrs Green and Charles.

For election purposes Monday was a bitterly cold day, and the agents of the various candidates had a bed time of it, exposed to the iacleaiency of the weather, which alternated from bright sunshine to cutting winds and driving snow. The emanate were in Town Hall and Viaduct Wards. the former having three candidates, Dr Latham, Mr GF Clarke, and Mr 0 Moon, and the latter two candidateds Mr J W Emmett, J.P.,and Mr D Williams. In the Town Hall Ward the fight settled down to a trial of strength between Dr Latham sod Mr Clarke, and the result showed that the struggle had been a keen one. The Viaduct Ward was to all intents and purposes a labour fight and it was in this ward that one of the greatest surprises experienced in the district turned up. Mr Emmett is the manager of the Viaduct Work', and Mr Williams is branch Secretary of the Amalgamated Engineers, and recently an employe at the Viaduct Works. On one side only much animus was shown whilst Mr Emmett, by an exceedingly narrow shave gained the seat, the close voting being evidently due to apathy on Mr Emmett's part. For the Viaduct Ward, the polling station was the District Schools, there being , two booths. The Town Hall polling station was at the Town Hall, two booths, and as we last week gave the names of the presiding officers and clerks there is no need to again publish them. Mr C Cole. Clerk to the Council was returning officer. The poll opened at 12 o'clock but the voting proceeded very slowly, the only brisk moments being between one and two o'clock, and after half-past five. On the stroke of eight the polling closed, and the ballot boxes were conveyed to an upper room of the Town Hall, where a staff of counters pro- ceeded to ascertain the result, which, about nine o'clock was declared as under. Town Hall Ward Latham Clarke
Moon

Emmett Williams Majority for Emmett l3 Mr Cole officially announced the numbers in the room, and Mr Emmett in moving a vote of thank; to that gentleman, referred to the impartial manner in which he had conducted the election. He was sure whether they were successful or not, they ought to be thankful to him for the way in which he had performed his duties. Dr. La:ham, in seconding the motion, said that en two occasions he load been the unsuccessful candidate, and on each occasion he had congratulated the presiding officer at the way he bad conducted the proceedings, and although Mr Cole had been amongst them only a short time he load been impressed with his desire to do his duty inonartially that day.—Other candidates sup. ported, and the motion was carried with acclamation: Mr Cole said it was an extreme pleasure to him to receive that vote of thanks. He had endeavoured to carry out the election impartially, as it was the duty of every retuning officer to do. (Hear, hear.) He then proceeded to the balcony and announced the figures to the waiting crowd the results being received with mingled cheers and booting. Messrs Emmett, Latham, Williams, Clarke, and Moon thanked the electors for their support. Mr Clarke said he had been defeated by a section of Town Hall Ward for whom be would not give a rap. He could not say that be would come forward again, but if Ihe did, he should not depend upon the support of renegades who tried to support every country but their own. (Cheers and hooting.) Mr Moon thanked the 24 electors who had voted for I him, remarking if they were satisfied he was.
