div.head: NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. [By " Ovalist.
div.p: NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. [By " Ovalist.

Warrington spilt a little more Yorkshire blood on Saturday when they took the sc sips of the Leech; Parish Churchmen, who did not succumb, however, without a game struggle. The battle was not q lite so sanguinary as all this might lead anyone to think, but it was thoroughly typical of cup-ties in general. There WAS fxitement in plenty during agreat portion of the game, which was far from being ono sided, though the result w*e 11 points to nil in favour of the home club. The Parish Church had some idea of avenging their fellow &lime who were slaughtered by Warrington in the first round but the task proved somewhat above their capacity.

For a full quarter of an hour Warrington had decided ! ly the worst of matters. The visitors played with the wind at their backs and by dint of making the game a forward one they soon had Warrington busy looking af7er the security of the goal line. The " wire pullers " were uot in it for real hard pushing and the bulky scrummager.; from Leeds did pretty much as they liked for a time. Things looked decidedly glaomy even though it was clear that the Parish backs wers not capable of I much in the scoring line. Warrington's defence stood the test well, however, and the line has not yet been (no ised in this svason's cup tournament. If they eon! I not hold their own indirect snrummaging. Warrington made up for much of the deficilacy by prompt heeling- out, and then the stsperiority of the barks told its tale. Once they had got a good footing in the Leeds half ,and the scoring commenced. Fish was the man to "open the ball" and the way he escaped the robust tacklers on the other side was well vvorth seeing. Though the goal kick failed the attempt was an excellent one for the ball bounced on the cross-bar and dropped on the wrong side. Even play followed to the interval when the position of the home team seemed moderately secure.

They soon made it evident that the Parish were in for a warm time in the second half. The forwards having succeeded in tiring the bigger men opposed to them, began to get a bit of their own back, and the attack was maintained, Parish Church shone on the defence, how— ever, and they well upheld the title of being one of the best) defensive teams in the bread-tcred county. Try as they would Warrington could not find an opening even by superior combination, so sure and certain was the" marking "of ihe Leeds backs. Time and per- severance told their tale eventually, and Isherwood added a second try, the credit for which was due in great part te the magnificent play of Bate and Duck- worth. Just on time Harris got his usual try by his own exertions, and Fish placed a goal frotn the most difficult angle possible. Parish Church, therefore, retired handsomely beaten, 11-0.

Warrington again maintained the high standard of foothill thoy have shown since the commencernect of the cup-tourney. Forward there was any amount of endui acme and speed, while the backs in the rear com- bined most effectively. The performance of the team all r mod was very satisfactory seeing that the visitors wera much the more powerful forward and coed affmd to play five threequarters and still hold their own in the packs. All three teams Warrington have met have had an extra back our, so that the Yorkshirernen are evidently getting a good idea of Warrington prowess in the scoring line. In the same connection there is another thing to be noted, and that is that Warrington aie not sufficiently weighty if their opponents Can always spare a forward for defensive work. It is very 'fortunate that the two Askam men were secured before Ithe commencement of the cup-ties.

I think Bob Bate was the best man on the Warrington side. ge played a game worthy of "Smack'. at his best, end had a lot to do with Warrington's victory. Duck- worth and he combined beautifully, and their complete understanding was worth a lot to the home team. All the three quarters played at the top of their form, the two centres doing very fine work. Dickenson again sbow:d his facility for dodging inwards at unexpected moments, which is the secret of true centre play. It is absolutely nece)sary, however, that either Harris or Isherwood should know of the move, for oftener than not on Saturday there was no one to take the pass. The fortnight's rest has done El4llam good,and he played one of his best games against the Churchmen. Boardman was the most prominent forward—in fact he was so prominent on two occasions that it is a miracle the referee did not have something to say to him. I would just caution the burly Latchford man against suffering Mort eon's fate.

The Parish Church team quite justified my predictions in regard to them by proving a difficult lot to beat. They had very much the same team as at Runcorn, and miley, the County half hack, and Evans were the best men on the side again. Neither is particularly smart, but 13th are strong and reliable and play the game. Corcoran was safe at full-hack, and the forwards did grand work. It needs something more than pure for. ward play to evre tries, however.

Thera was an excellent "gate" again, the weather h.ing very favourable to football. The proceeds were £l5B. all but something like £3O coming from the " six- penny" side; which was packed. Whatever else happens Warrington should have a nice bank balance as the result of the cup-ties.

Bradford just managed to get the better of Wakefield Trinity after all, oae point only separating them at the finish. I rather fancied the Trinitarians and the lint that they had four fifths of th play justifies the fancy. The Yorkshire Oa mpiona have done nothing very great since they oefeatei Swinton, and Warrington should entertain them to-day with feelings of confidence.

Other ties"were a bit surprising, though not much. Batley won at S. Helene, and got mobbed for their presumption—a little matter which is likely to cost the Saints dear from what I hear. Oldham upset predictions by taking the Broughton Rangers down, and in no uncertain fashion either. They seem to have an eye on both " pots." Widnes won at Birkenhead, and accomplished a very creditable performance, while Runcorn massacred the Yorkists without much diffi• culty. Kingston Rovers won at Brighouse, and Castle- ford got the better of Dewsbury.
The Tykes therefore, have four teams in the last eight, Lstmashire three and Cheshire one. To-Asy's contests for a place in the semi-finals are as follow : Warrington • Bradford. VVidnas v Oldham.

div.head: Batley v Runcorn: Hull Kingston Rovers v Castleford.
div.p: Batley v Runcorn: Hull Kingston Rovers v Castleford.
To-day's Big Match.
There has been no such excitement in town 'aban

U etball since the year Warrington got in the ssmi-flnals by d ,feiting the then crank Yorkshire team—Halifax. Tose was a great game and one still hears allusions to the intense suspense of the home crowd during the time gslifas pressed continuously for 20 minutes within ten yards of the home line. It was not only a great game hut it was witnessed by a great crowd,rhe receipts being £199 8;. That total should be easily exceeded to-day when the Bradfordians come to Wilderspool in their all - conquering might. There are a great many people Icoming from Yorkshire if the weather keeps fine.and the whole of South West Lancashire is sure to contribute its quota, for there is no 7striq hereabouts to compote with it for importance and attraction.

Bradford are, a great team, and include in their ranks no less than five Biglish international players, four of whom are in the back division. They are Ward, (full backl ; Cooper (centrP) ; Marsden and Wood, (halves); and T BroadlPy (cotain, forward). Among the things I heard last Saturday was that Bradford bad five for- wards weighing 14 stones or more. Nevertheless Wakefield Trinity boat them in the scrimmages, and there is no reason why Warrington should not have a considerable say in the control of the ball.

I have no hesitation in tipping Warrington to win. They play such a desperate game on their own soil and have improved so much of late that it is too much to admit the ability of any t-iim to come here and gain the honours. Bradford might ,io the trick, of clime, but I Fancy they will meet fheir miteh this time. Certainly they will meet fifteen triers.

Warrington will be represented by the team which has done duty for the past fortnigbt. Hallam, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenenn and Harris, threequarters ; BateTand Duckworth, half-backs; Boardman, Fell, Ed- mondson, Elea, Scholtze, Mereweather, Cunningham, and Swift, forwards.

Bradford have done their bent to get the match trans- ferred tl Park Avenue, but Warrington were above temptation, handsome though the terms were. The Bradford executive offered £2OO and half the proceeds over £4OO. As the "gate" would almost certainly have been £5OO, this was equal to an offer of £2so—a sum large enough to have tempted most clubs. Jr says much for the loyalty of the Warrington committee, to the players and supporters that they unanimously rejected the offer, and would probably have done so had it been double the amount.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Council was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. r J Knowles preiidel. There were also present .—Admiral Joae-- Parry, Messrs S Woo.: ward, J Melntyrl, J Stokes, 0 E Lmaker, T Wright, J M)seley Williams, r Baxter, H Talbot, P Weave, .J Spruce, W Flerehe.r, J Bolshaw E A Wallinvton, 8 Horton, E Clarke, T antwiss, E Brether- ton, J Niokson, P Leather, a Mawdsley,T Darlington, T LewiQ. George Pilau, J 341unfteld, with Mr Ge-mge F Ashton (clerk), Mr W E llrngb (assistant clerk), Mr I James Farrington (inspector), Mr Swinton (surveyor), i sad Dr J Adams (medical officer.
WORK FOR THE NEW COUNCIL. TUE ISOLATION HOSPITAL QUESTION.

The Local (1 merriment B iard wra—te enclosing a aolri, of a letter addresied to them by Mr Francis Boson. of Frodsharn, and adverting to the ,•tatement of 'he Medical Officer of flealth, on page 21 of his annul reoort for 1899, for the Rural District, and enquire 1 how the questi aof hospital provision for the district now stands P
Admiral Parry : There is no question as to our need of an isolation hospital. Only at the last meeting Mr tiloseley-Williams had recounted to us hoar great the need was. And--

Mr Wbodward (interposing) : We want one at Thel- wall ? (Laughter), Admiral Parry : Well, yes we do. (Laughter.) I think we do want something of the kind. Diphtheria and such things kill, and Ido not want to ho killed sooner than I can help. (Laughter.) Mr. Moseley Williams pointed out bow he had laboured in the din ction of having such an hospital,but he had been so completely blocked and baulked in the matter that he was nearly sick of it. At the last naeet- iag he spoke very feelingly, and they would remember he had recounted to them a little of his experiencos of running up lead down the country seeking accommoda- tion in some hospital, but the cases could not be accom• modated in Chester, Warrington or Runcorn: And there was fully £2O expended, a certain six weeks of discomfort ; and, afterwards, came the disinfecting and messing about. If that was his experience, he asked whatever was to become of the poor cottage people who could not do as he had done? He thought it was de- plorable that they were responsible for the disease, loss, and illness of the children, and certainly they would be responsible for the loss, suffering, and deaths which had arisen and would arise until something was done. He would not add anything further only say, that he for one objected to the letter being ignored. As he had stated on a former occ ision the question for them was " were they going to do it, or not ?" (Hear, hear.) Mr Woodward questioned who were the real obstruc- tors ? Did not the obstruction come from the Local Government Board itself ? Of his own knowledge, he knew they had considered more than one site for the purposes of an Isolation Hospital, and the Board refus them. Was it right that they should be driven from pillar to post, in order to satisfy the Local Government Board ? But for them, the District Council would cer- tainly have moved in the matter more than three years I ago. Dr Adams, said, if allowed, he would like to say a word or two on the question. The District Council had shown its entire willingness to accede to his suggestion for the erection of an Iselation Hospital as set forth in various medical reports from 1894 to the present year. The Council had lo ,ked for sites and done everything ; only, when Mr Da! Zie gave the Council to understand , that certain sites.—which were not a mile from any dwelling house, he thought it was—would not receive the sanction of the Local Government Board they desisted As a matter of fact, no distinct proposal, had gone from the Clerk's office to the Local Government Board: floe Clerk said that was SO.

Dr Adams, continuing, pointed out that the Council should have forwarded to the Local Government Board plans showing the propinquity of dwelling-houses to the , proposed site. The Council knew him well enough to know that he was not saying all this in a spirit of blaming the , Council ; and, if the Local Government Board was to believe that the Council was in earnest, the Council I should take the necessary steps for laying such a plan as I would be drawn up under his advice, or the advice of ' any person or Committee that the Council might appoint More the Local Government Board. The Local Govern- ment Board would then know the exact provision the District Council could make, and could either sanction or dispose of the Imlation Hospital question altogether. He could not go back on the reports he had submitted to the Council in 1894, and subsequent years, and he could not say that the Isolation Hospital Wag not required. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the statement made by Mr Danzia, the doctor pointed out that as a nastier of fact there was not an Isolation Hospital erected which was one mile off the nearest dwelling-house. Admiral Parry said from what the doctor had said it , was very clear they bad not moved in the matter at all. The Doctor suggested that some membars of the Council should propose the re-appointment of the old Isolation Hospital Committee, and that the whole matter be again gone on with. Mr. Woodward rose to give the necessary notice of motion; but, took the opportunity of informing Admiral Parry he was sorry fol. misleading him. He wanted to ask a question, however. There was a site near Tunne Top, not far from that house,—viewed, by a Com- mittee of which he himself was a member ; if it was only the opinion of Mr Danzie in his personal capacity that made them give up the consideration of that, site, what right had the Committee to leave that site, and go and view other sites P The necessary notice of motion was given. _ _

Mr. Lioaker bore out what Mr Woodward had stated with regard to site viewing, for he had been approacheJ as to the price of land. Dr. Adams recalled the reason for the abandonment of that particular site, as its nearness to the Workhouse. - The next businev was then proceeded with.

div.head: FRODSII&M LORDSHIP AFFAIRS.
div.p: FRODSII&M LORDSHIP AFFAIRS.

The Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committee, met on the 25th March,at the Boys' Schoolroom, Ovezton,under the presidency of Mr A Thomas.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board, adverting to the Rural District Council's request for ssnction to borrow £3OB for purposes of water supply for Frodsham Lordship,and requesting further information.—The Clerk intimated that the inform‘tion requested bad been forwarded.—lt was resolved that the Clerk be paid £2O for his services during the past year.—After discussion the committee declined to pin with the Frodsham Township in the matter of providing fire appliances for use in two parishes.

div.head: SIR J. T. BRUNNER AND TUE PURE HEIR BILL.
div.p: SIR J. T. BRUNNER AND TUE PURE HEIR BILL.

Mr W H Young, secretary to Sir John T Brunner, Bart.. M.P., wrote as follows :—" Sir John Brunner de- sires me to say that he has come to the conclusion that your Act is right about the matter of Pure Beer, and to tell you that it is his Intention to give his support to the Pure Beer Bill introduced this session by Mr Purvis."

Tire THELWALL NDISANCE.—TRE DOCTOR'S DEFENCE. The Clerk read the following letter, " The Stables, Cuerden Hall, Thelwall, near Warrington, March 25th to Mr Ashton. Sir,—How many more appeals will have to be made before anything is done to prevent such sick- ness as we suffer from and which is directly attributed to living in the bad smells from the Grappenhall tan- yard? How Would any of your Council like it if the same vile smell entered their dwelling at any hour of the night or day, and caused them to be so sick that to sleep I was an impossibility ; and, to work, bordering on the same lines. Four weeks ago we had to call the doctor lin again for severe sickness caused by such a strong 'putrid smell, from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m., coaling from the Lanyard into our cottage. The doctor, on see- ing us, said the bad smells would have to be stopped lor else we should all be stretched out , through it. Again on Thursday week, driving past the tanyard tanks, I got such a dose at vile stench in my throat, that, for four days, every mouthful of food I ate tasted so strongly of the same rank matter,' that it caused me to vomit all food again. So von may judge how severe are its effects on those so unfortunate as to get a dose of such an undesirable stench.! can truly say that for the last eighteen months I have been rumble to follow up my work a third part of the time through sickness by these smells from the tanyard. On the morning of the 17th March, as Mrs Tinkler went from here, she got a dose of the same sort of bad smell that made her throat and chest sore, and up to the 20th she told us she still had the same had smell in her throat. Mrs Tickler is the person who wrote to you complaining of the bad smell here coming from the tanyard at your last Council meeting; after she had been here nursing my wife. We have complained repeatedly to Dr Adams,the Medical Officer for the district, of the bad smells we get and I think it was hardly a proper thing for him on the last occasion I saw him in our cottage, to call me a "liar," when I was explaining how quickly the smell came. We are not the only persons who complain of the bad smells from the tan yard, for only on Saturday last 15 people were witnesses of its vileness from 5 p.m. to 10.30 p.m.,ene person being sick on the road through the stench." Mr J Vickers, Temperance Rouge, Theiwall, also writing with regard to the above, said he worked in i Warrington, and lived n the village,so that his wife and children might get the benefit of the fresh country air, but the atmosphere at Thel wall Was worse polluted than that of any town he knew. The nature of his work compelled him to return borne at all hours of;the day'and night, but whatever that hour may be the air was per- vaded with the sickening odours from the tanyard. He had complained to Dr Adame,who said the Council would not do what he s.)egested, hence that letter. 'They had no sickness before the alteration in the system of tan- ing, but since then diphtheria and other diseases were only too commontand they had noticed that each visita- tion was always preceded by a particularly bad smell:from the tanneries. He was not the only sufferer; groat numbers of people complained, and many had been made ill. On the previous Saturday the stench was simply abomin- able, and unless they had an alteration speedily, he was afraid that the results would be disastrous. There was

an awful responsibility resting upon the Ccuacil in thiS matter, and he begged of them to treat it with all seriousness and urgency. Ile himself had lost two cbl dren during the present year, as the result, he was firmly convinced, of that atrocious nuisance. Othi'r children, had died of the same dread disease (diphtheria), and unless they acted quickly, others might follow. He wag a bricklayer himself, and had had great experience ia drains, and there was nothing in that way around there to account for the smells complained of. If the Council would kindly take the subject in hand they would be doing invaluable service to the neighbourhood. Mr Woodward, when the Clerk bad commenced read° in the second letter, asked if the matter was in tfte hands of the Local Government Board. The Chairman: replied it was, and the letter was sub. sequently read through. Mr Linaker :—How long is the matter ening to goon? I for one think there is just ground for complaint throughout the district, whether from the tanneries or the sewers lam not prepared to say, but I do think these is a terrible Smell.

Wallington agreed with Mr Linaker. Th-e wag a terrible smell, and as time went on and the weather grew hotter it was likely to become more intense. Fla moved that the Clerk write to the Local Gr.veransent Board asking that they should give the subject their immediate attention, and get to the bottom of tha matter.

Mr Woodward agreed to that course. Dr Adams, wished to make an observation, and hoped a note would be taken of his remarks. They ought to clearly define their podtion. At the present moment the Local Government Board's inquiry was pending, and it appeared to him c that he was entitled to call the atten- tion of the District Council, to certain recommendationS he had made from time to time, and which if carried out would have solved the matter. Firstly, that the Tannery effluent should be purified as far as possible, and secondly, he had made the recommendation. he wail not speaking then of the joint report of Dr V icher and himself, but of his own report, that the ditch should be piped, and the old conditions of affairs there abolished. If the owner of Cuerden Hall bad abolished a water Course, which W4s the ditch betweeo Thelwall and Grappenhall, he (Dr Adams) saw no reason why the District Council should not abolish another. Another of his suggestions WAS to have all the sewerage pipes headed to one point and tank at The,' wall, and if they had a chamber ventilated by a sniff' ciently high shaft they would dispose of the whole of the sewage question on a scientific basis. That afas the iohs Woos of the recommendations be made before Dr. Vector came in at all, and the District Council up to the present had not seen their way to carry them out. That was the reason they were where they were. It well nothing but a common ditch, and only required coin' man drainage ; there was nothing especial about it, onlf the amount of correspondence. (Laughter). Mr Wallington, (to the doctor :)—Do you really tbinit that it is injurious to health ? I Dr Adams: I think that all sewage—domestic sewage.'" The Chairman called Mr Wallington to order. Mr Wallington : Very well sir, but Ido think that ought to be allowed to ask the Medical Officer questions P I The Chairman : I have a proposi ion before the Council that the Local Government Board be written to.. This was seconded, and carried. THE amoral FOOTPATH. The Clerk said that a new aspect had been thrown on the question of the obstruction of the footpath at Moore, as reported by MP Gleave, for Mr J R Smethurst, ef the District Estate Office, Lime-street Station.Liverpaol,hatt answered two of his letters to the effect that he found that the Ship Canal deviation was carried out by the Ship Canal Company, and any question as Co the foot' way at Moore should be taken up with them. Be (g! Ashton) originally thought there was an obstruction ; it there was a deviation it was entirely another matter and would have to be enquired into. A committee of Messrs Gleave, Darlington, and Rol', lince,with the Clerk,was subsequently appointed to deal with the subject.

Southport—Conservative Club. The return match was played at Warrington el Saturday.
